speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: MR. PEARSON    REFERENCE TO PRESS REPORT OF REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE IN SENATE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege affecting the members of this house. It arises out of a report in the press of a statement made in the other place about the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Jung) with reference to his racial origin.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. PEARSON    REFERENCE TO PRESS REPORT OF REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE IN SENATE
speechtext: Order. I rather anticipated that point might be raised. Some hon. members have already spoken to me about it. In my view a question of privilege cannot properly be raised against a member of the other house for something said in the other house. The other house has its privileges just as we have, and its powers over its own members to deal with their conduct in the other house. It does not seem to me to be appropriate to raise, as a matter of privilege, something said by a member of the other house when this house has no power to deal with the matter. I do not say that it is not a proper matter for comment at a proper time or that one cannot refer to or cite the proceedings of the other house. However, I do not think it is appropriate to raise what the hon. member has in mind as a matter of privilege.

subtopic: MR. PEARSON    REFERENCE TO PRESS REPORT OF REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE IN SENATE
speechtext:
Of course, Mr. Speaker, I
accept your ruling; but as this statement in the other house referred to a member of this house, and as this statement has appeared in the press under headlines which I think are derogatory to the members of this house, I had thought and hoped I could bring it forward in this way under these circumstances.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subtopic: MR. PEARSON    REFERENCE TO PRESS REPORT OF REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE IN SENATE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would think that the person who might raise the matter, if it can be raised at all, would be the hon. member for Vancouver Centre. Whether he will entertain the same resentment as do members as a whole will remain for him to say when he comes here. In any event the matter could be discussed next week in a general way when the subject of external affairs is up for consideration. I feel that Mr. Jung-and I refer to him as Mr. Jung-should be here when this matter is referred to because whatever answer he gives will be in keeping with the tradition that we are all Canadians.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. PEARSON    REFERENCE TO PRESS REPORT OF REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE IN SENATE
speechtext: As this is a rather novel matter, perhaps I might take it under further consideration. May I say that I appreciate what hon. members have said.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we greatly appreciate the attitude Your Honour has taken on this matter. However, there is one point which has not been mentioned by you but which we feel means a great deal, and it is this. If a reflection is made on a member of the House of Commons, is that then not a matter of privilege in the House of Commons?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the Leader of the Opposition asked whether I could make a statement regarding the discussions which took place as between the President and Secretary of State of the United States, various members of the government and myself. While I have not had an opportunity during the intervening hours to make very much preparation in this regard, I will outline in general the discussions which took place, leaving, however, detailed discussion until the debate on external affairs which is set for next week.
The members of this house and our fellow citizens in this city have shown very clearly how happy they were to welcome the President of the United States to Ottawa. A visit of this kind is an opportunity for us to demonstrate the ties of history and kinship which bind us together, and I know we were all very pleased to have the President address this house. He stated his views frankly and in a straightforward manner, as we have done for this government. We appreciated
2140	HOUSE OF
Discussions with President Eisenhower the opportunity to hear him explain the views of his country on those important issues which are of consequence to both our nations. Nothing better illustrates the strength of our relationship than that we can talk honestly to each other without endangering the association which holds us together.
The same spirit which was evidenced in this house was also apparent during the discussions between the President and the Secretary of State of the United States, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, other ministers and myself. We were aided by the presence of Mr. Dulles, who shared with us his broad experience and wide grasp of the problems of international relations. He had just returned from Paris and was able to give us a general idea as to the attitude of France respecting the great problems which particularly affect her and those which affect Canada jointly with France as members of NATO.
I think what has taken place illustrates the need of some continuing body to permit of a general discussion from time to time of our respective points of view. Respecting the earlier reference to the need for arrangements to permit of discussion from time to time between members of the congress of the United States and the parliament of Canada, while constitutionally as far as the President is concerned no decision in that regard could, of course, be achieved, the success of the meeting in general, as a meeting between the President and myself and the others to whom I have referred, indicates how very important it is that something in the nature of an exchange of opinions should take place from time to time as between the parliament of our country and the congress of the United States. My hope is that the recommendations which were made by the committee composed of Congressmen Hays and Coffin will be accepted; that a committee on Canadian-United States relations will be set up in the United States congress, and that we in our House of Commons will set up a similar committee, and that from time to time mutual exchanges will take place between members of these committees or between members of parliament and members of congress outside those committees, to the end that in general discussion the views of each nation may be ascertained and thereby, through discussions, causes of disagreement removed.
As far as the general discussions which took place are concerned, the President and I touched upon most of the pressing issues of the day as well as upon matters of more particular bilateral interest. There was very broad agreement on these fundamental issues, and whatever differences we may


have on details there was never any question either before these meetings or during them-nor will there be, I know, in the days ahead-that either of our nations will lose sight of the fact that we must remain united in our objectives and in our determination if freedom is to be maintained.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs and I discussed with President Eisenhower and Mr. Dulles such matters as progress toward disarmament and the changing nature of Soviet policy with reference to the economic challenge of the critical situation in the Middle East. The Minister of National Defence had an opportunity to talk over our mutual defence problems with Mr. Dulles. The Minister of Finance and the Minister of Agriculture discussed trade and economic questions, and the Minister of Public Works and the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources had a talk on the problem of boundary waters. In addition to these more formal talks there were, of course, opportunities for a less formal exchange of views in the atmosphere of the social occasions during which we met.
With respect to the international situation, members of the house are aware that discussions have taken place during the last year or so with regard to the providing of safeguards against the danger of surprise attack, and Canadians and Americans have a particular and special interest in these arrangements for the polar regions. These matters were discussed with reference to the recent letter which Mr. Khrushchev sent to the President signifying Soviet readiness in principle to enter into direct discussions on the technical aspects of the problem of preventing surprise attack.
Hon. members will not expect me to indicate even in general terms the contents of the President's contemplated reply, but that its broad purpose is to bring about such technical talks will be evident from our agreement that experts should work together on this problem. Studies have been under way for some time, and I understand that similar work has also been done in the United States. The meaning of our agreement is not only that there should be consultation between our officials; such exchanges of views on disarmament matters have long been a feature of our normal relations. It signifies rather that in the immediate future our collaboration should concentrate in a practical way on this particular and very important matter.
As to the general question of defence, it has been the aim and purpose of this government-and I think that view has been accepted by the Canadian people as a whole- that at all times in our joint defence efforts

we must assure and maintain over and above every other consideration the political and civilian control with respect to military matters. During the course of the President's visit we reviewed the complex issues which arise from the joint efforts of our two governments in the field of continental defence. There was mutual recognition of the increased necessity for regular consultation between our two governments, both on the specific requirements with which the two governments may expect to be faced in providing for the security of North America and on international events which could lead to the necessity of activating the continental air defences. There was full realization that our joint efforts in the defence of North America must continue to serve the objectives of the NATO alliance in which we have banded together with other like-minded countries in the search for collective security in an uneasy world.
In these discussions we took note of the intimate co-operation of our two countries over the past two decades in matters relating to continental defence and of the machinery which had been established to provide for the consideration of defence problems of common concern. We recognized that these interdependent defence relationships must continue and, indeed, that they would become even more important and more complex in the face of the advanced weapon technology which is now available to potential aggressors. We agreed that while existing machinery in the defence field had served us well in the past and would undoubtedly continue to do so in the future, the need existed to supplement existing channels for consultation by providing for a periodic review at the ministerial level of problems which might be expected to arise. We recognized that decisions in this field would involve not only consideration of the military aspects of our common defence but also political and economic factors. We thought it particularly important as well that every step should be taken to maintain the principle and the fact of civilian control and guidance of these common military activities.
We agreed therefore that we should establish a joint ministerial committee to be known as the Canada-United States committee on joint defence, with scope to consider all matters bearing on the common defence of the North American continent. This committee will consist for Canada of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, the Minister of National Defence and the Minister of Finance; and for the United States of the Secretary of State, the Secretary of Defence
11, 1958	2141
Discussions with President Eisenhower and the Secretary of the Treasury. We agreed that such other appropriate cabinet members as either government might designate from time to time might participate on an ad hoc basis in the committee's deliberations. The committee will normally meet alternately in Washington and Ottawa under the chairmanship of the Secretary of State when the meeting is held in the United States and of the Secretary of State for External Affairs when the meeting is held in Canada.
In regard to the question of defence production, we examined together the situation which arises in these days of mounting defence costs and the need for rationalizing whenever possible and consistently with national requirements the industrial base for our own defence needs. In anticipation of a meeting of the newly-announced committee at cabinet level on defence matters, some consideration has been given to the sort of items which might be placed upon the agenda. Further consideration, of course, will have to be given in consultation with our colleagues in each country to prepare ourselves to discuss in adequate detail many of these matters.
That in general represented the tenor of the discussions with respect to the subject of defence. So far as particulars are concerned, they will be available in committees; in the committee on defence, as an example, when the minister might be asked further questions with respect thereto.
I now come to the problem of economic questions. Consideration was given to the principal economic issues that are now facing the free world. It was agreed that some of those have become intensified by the Soviet economic offensive. It is more important now than ever before that measures be considered which might be expected to strengthen the economies of countries in the free world through the expansion of international trade and the promotion of programs of economic development. If progress can be made in these directions, as I believe it can, it may become easier to make fully convertible the main currencies in which world trade is conducted; but it would be quite wrong to suggest, as one newspaper did this morning, that any plans had been agreed upon, or been determined in part, with respect to convertibility of sterling since, of course, such action is entirely for decision by Her Majesty's government in the United Kingdom.
We received from the President and his Secretary of State reports concerning the prospects for the trade agreements legislation. We described the preparations being made for
2142	HOUSE OF
Discussions with President Eisenhower the commonwealth trade and economic conference. Within those limits various matters were discussed, all of which, of course, cannot be referred to at this time. However, there is one matter of particular interest and that is the necessity, as we see it in Canada, of revising the list of strategic materials which come under either prohibition or control for export to the Soviet bloc and to communist China. This matter is going to be considered at length at a conference that is about to take place in Paris of representatives of nations of the free world.
I raised with the President the question that some Canadian subsidiaries of United States companies may have been prevented from accepting orders from communist China, or from peoples in that country, by the application of United States foreign assets control regulations, even though acceptance of such orders would be permitted by the policy of the Canadian government. The President expressed the view that the United States regulations should not be applied in any way to the disadvantage of the Canadian economy. If cases arose in the future where the refusal of orders by companies operating in Canada might have any effect on Canadian economic activity, the United States government would consider favourably exempting the parent company in the United States from the application of the foreign assets control regulations with respect to such orders.
It was made perfectly clear, and I want to underline this fact, that there was no question at any time that, with respect to the operations of Canadian companies, Canadian law shall govern and Canadian wishes shall be respected. Further consideration of this question will naturally require some days. I go no further at this time except to reunderline what I have said to re-emphasize the stand taken by this government, that Canada as a sovereign nation has the right to the maintenance in its full amplitude of its legislative enactments, both dominion and provincial.
I think that in general is a summary of- not in particular-the discussions that took place. I must say that during the course of the three days I was more than ever impressed with the very reasonable and cooperative attitude that was taken to assure that at all times anything that takes place in the economic field which might conceivably cause difficulty to either of our countries will to the limit of our respective capacities be resolved to the end that our unity shall be maintained; that in whatever we do there will be a full realization on the part of each of us that in taking our individual courses
[Mr. Diefenbaker.I

as individual nations every regard and respect will be paid to the fullest consideration that nothing that is done shall detrimentally affect the other country; and that indeed we now approach an era internationally where it becomes more important than ever before that the nations of the free world must, in the interests of survival itself, bring about economic changes in unity that might 15 or 20 years ago have been regarded as impossible of achievement.
I conclude by saying in very simple words that this conference did represent a forward step. There was a spirit of mutual respect and forbearance and a common desire to arrive at decisions which will assure that the unity that we all desire to attain will be preserved, and that the sovereignty of each of our countries will not be impinged upon in any way.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of ihe Opposition):
speechtext:
I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that the members of the house-certainly we on this side-are grateful to the Prime Minister for his statement, and all the more so because he has not had very much time in which to prepare it after coming, I suppose, straight to the house from seeing off the President and Secretary of State. We will, as the Prime Minister has said, have an opportunity next week in the discussion of external affairs to go into these matters in greater detail, because their importance certainly justifies that discussion.
We on this side of the house share the satisfaction of the Prime Minister and his colleagues in the good results which have been achieved during this visit. We share with him the pleasure of having had in our capital at this time the President and Secretary of State. I am sure the conversations between the Prime Minister and President have been fruitful and useful, just as those between the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the Secretary of State have been.
The Prime Minister has indicated that some new prices of international machinery have developed out of this meeting. He made reference to the joint committee on defence which is being set up. This should, I think, be a useful development, though speaking as one who has had some experience with international machinery in recent years, just as is the case with other such pieces of machinery this will be as valuable and as useful as the participants desire to make it. I am glad the Prime Minister mentioned the desirability of a joint committee of parliament and congress being set up. This is a matter which was recommended from the United States side by Congressmen Hays and Coffin in their

report, and by Senator Aiken. It was referred to also by the Prime Minister in the United States a few weeks ago.
I cannot think, myself, of anything at this time which might be more useful than such a joint committee. I quite realize that this is a matter concerning which the President would have to be very careful in his talks with the Prime Minister because of the division of powers in Washington. Nevertheless, perhaps the initiative which has been taken could be followed up on the legislative level, and something permanently useful could result.
I noticed with much interest the Prime Minister's reference to the economic aspects of his talks. I agree with him that too much stress cannot be placed on the necessity for expanding trade, not only in the interests of the prosperity of the countries concerned but because the necessity to expand trade in the free world will perhaps become more and more important as a defence against the kind of aggression from the other world which reflects itself not so much now in aggression across borders as in aggression in markets. The Prime Minister, I think, was quite right when he mentioned that one aspect of this expansion is convertibility, though neither the President nor the Prime Minister, or their governments, can themselves bring about this convertibility. It is one of the objectives they both have in mind. It is an objective which might be encouraged and sought at the forthcoming commonwealth economic conference.
The Prime Minister mentioned that from .time to time difficulties arise between our two countries because of our differing regulations in regard to trade with the communist countries. It seems to me, and I know the Minister of Trade and Commerce must be very much aware of this, that the sooner we can agree among the NATO countries-I know talks are going on to this end-on a uniform list of commodities which are on the strategic list and therefore not exportable to countries which we fear, the sooner those difficulties will disappear.
This question of the China differential has been before us now for years, and the sooner it can be cleared up the better. This morning the Prime Minister said, and it was a very interesting part of his statement, that he felt sure as a result of these talks-I do not want to misquote him or say anything which does not reflect his meaning. However, I gathered the impression that he felt sure that the difficulties which have developed in one or two cases over the export of goods to communist China can be cleared away by the application of United States law in such a way that it will not prevent Canadian
11. 1958	2143
Discussions with President Eisenhower subsidiaries of United States companies from exporting goods to other countries if that is within our laws and our regulations. I am sure that must be a welcome development to all members of this house. It was therefore with some mild disappointment that I read in the press conference report last night that the spokesman of the United States delegation was not able to go any further in his statement than to say that in these matters consultation would take place when difficulties arose.
The Prime Minister referred to the initiative that has perhaps been taken-one is never quite sure in these matters whether or not a genuine initiative has been taken- by the Soviet government with regard to technical discussions for the prevention of surprise attack. I am sure that members of the house will have heard with great satisfaction that both the Canadian government and the United States government are determined to follow up this move in case it turns out to be a valuable and useful initiative. It is, of course, something that has been in the minds of the Canadian government for a long time, especially in its relationship to Arctic defence. It is encouraging to know that the reaction in Washington and in Ottawa-and I am sure in London and Paris -has been quick and positive to what may turn out to be a useful move.
I am sure that the talks that have now been concluded have been carried on with that frankness which is characteristic of a tried and tested friendship such as that which exists and must be maintained between our two countries. It has been said that neighbourhood is a geographical fact but that neighbourliness is a relationship between people. I feel certain, Mr. Speaker, that the talks which have just been, concluded have deepened and strengthened that neighbourliness which is now more essential than ever in both countries in the tense and dangerous world in which we live.

Mr. Speaker, the members of this group listened with anticipation, interest and attention to the Prime Minister's preliminary and, naturally under the circumstances, brief review of the discussions with President Eisenhower and his colleagues. Naturally there is great interest in what the Prime Minister had to say this morning because of the great concern in Canada with the many problems that face us at the present time-I refer to our difficulties with respect to defence; disarmament; markets for lead, zinc, copper and other metals; markets for oil; markets for wheat and many other Canadian commodities-and also, Mr. Speaker, because of the growing interest and concern with respect

Discussions with President Eisenhower to the settlement of the issues between us and the United States concerning the development of boundary waters.
The substance of the arrangements reported by the Prime Minister, in the opinion of this group, will be revealed only after discussion on the estimates of the Department of External Affairs, after further explanations and details are given by the Secretary of State for External Affairs and as a result of action taken in the days ahead by the governments to meet the problems that concern us all.

On the orders of the day:

I should like to ask the Prime Minister a question arising out of his extremely informative statement to the house a few moments ago. Can the Prime Minister say definitely whether or not in the future a Canadian company like the Ford Motor Company would have the right to export automobiles to China? Would the Prime Minister also say what consultation took place on the question of Canadian oil exports to the United States and whether, as a result of this conference, anything is being done or is likely to be done to increase the market for Canadian oil, a very important point for many geographical areas in this country?

In so far as the last question is concerned, Mr. Speaker, I may say that there was discussion respecting oil and also the other matters to which the Leader of the Opposition made reference a few moments ago. While discussions took place and while representations were made, I do not think there is any useful information I can give on these questions at this time. There will be a meeting shortly, I hope, of the members of the economic committee, when in particular these questions will be discussed. During our talks naturally they were dealt with at some length in general between the President and myself but, of course, in detail as between the Minister of Trade and Commerce, the Minister of Finance and the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
However, as to oil, I can say that the problem is a difficult and complex one. We placed before the United States representatives most strongly the position of the oil industry within our country and the need of the amelioration of any unnecessary embargo or reduction in import by the United States. These discussions are still continuing. As I say, these matters cannot be determined in a matter of a few hours or

a few days. However, the fullest discussion took place with regard thereto with, of course, the realization by this government of the need of markets being extended and expanded not only for oil but also in respect of other products of Canadian mines. Without going into detail, I would mention in general iron, lead, zinc, copper and also aluminum and nickel.
And wheat?

I was dealing with the others. As one who was raised in the west, I may say that wheat never gets too far away from my thinking.
As to the first question, I would say that while the discussions were, naturally, particularly directed to the export of Ford cars, I was rather surprised to read this morning in a statement purported to have been made by the president of the Ford company that at no time was there anything in the nature of finality, and there was apparently no more, as I understood his statement, than some negotiations and discussions. I do express the hope that if the Ford company can secure an order from communist China it will be able to ship the cars.

Might I ask the Prime Minister if it was clear from the discussions between the President of the United States and himself that the directions of the United States in this matter are simply pursuant to treasury regulations, or do they involve any act on the part of congress itself?

I would say at this moment that the situation comes within the expression used by the hon. gentleman. If the regulations are dependent upon immediate congressional action in the United States- by a congress seemingly more desirous of an early conclusion of the session than is sometimes apparent in this house-I would think that any such legislation which might be introduced during the current session of congress would not have much hope of being passed.

Mr. Speaker, may I ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs if, with regard to the joint ministerial committee on defence, it will be within the terms of reference of that committee to include consideration not only of defence matters as such but the related matter of civil defence? Could the Secretary of State for External Affairs also give some information to the house as to why the Minister of Defence Production should not be included as one of the Canadian ministers on the proposed joint international ministerial body?

speakeroldname: Hon. Sidney E. Smith (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with respect to the first part of the hon. member's question having to do with civil defence, there was no discussion of that matter in the discussion concerning the setting up of this committee. I have the text of the announcement given to the press, and the committee will consult on matters bearing upon the common defence of the North American continent which lies within the North Atlantic treaty area. I believe it could well be demonstrated that civil defence bears on military defence. It could well be that civil defence could be discussed in the committee. I do not contemplate that in the meetings of that committee we will abide by strict rules of procedure; it will be a forum for a discussion of common problems in the field designated by the announcement.
With respect to the second part of the question raised by the hon. member for Essex East, as has been indicated to the house, this is going to be a six man committee, but I would draw his attention particularly to this paragraph:	"Other ministers may
participate on an ad hoc basis on a request by the committee." I can well anticipate that the Minister of Defence Production will be called into the discussion from time to time.

May I ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs whether it is anticipated that the present joint defence board, Canada-United States, will report to this proposed joint defence cabinet committee?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That has not been considered. I draw the attention of hon. members to this statement: "The committee will not supplant but will supplement existing joint boards and committees." I can well anticipate that at the military level -there are two other committees which provide for consultation across the border at military level, so there are three altogether, including the joint defence board- on occasion we will have to get the views of those two committees.

speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
maintopic: DELIVERY QUOTA POSITION IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to thank the hon. member for having given me notice of this question, and for deferring it for 24 hours when I informed him that I was assembling this information. I welcome the question, because the reply is very favourable indeed. Other hon. members from western Canada have asked me about this quota position.
The first part of the question is, what progress is being made toward the equalization of delivery quotas. The answer is, excellent progress. There are in the western provinces 2,070 delivery points to which the farmers bring their grain. Ninety per cent of those are now on a 6-bushel quota or have completed the 6-bushel quota. The figures are as follows: on the 5-bushel quota, 71 points; on the 6-bushel quota, 1,967 points; completed or closed, 32 points, for a total of 2,070.
The breakdown by provinces is as follows: All the 375 delivery points in Manitoba are now on a 6-bushel quota. In Saskatchewan 67 are on a 5-bushel quota, 1,026 on a 6-bushel quota, and 28 are closed. In Alberta four are on the 5-bushel quota, 562 are on the 6-bushel quota and four are closed. In British Columbia, where there are four delivery points, all are on the 6-bushel quota.
The second part of the question asked whether all producers would have an opportunity to deliver an equal quota by the end of the crop year. I think the figures I have given indicate that this will likely be the case.
The final part of the question asks whether in the light of the present marketing and crop conditions the quota may be raised to eight bushels or more. It is obvious that present marketing conditions are very good. Our exports of wheat will exceed the 300 million bushel target which was set last summer, and because of the large volume of exports these marketings from the farms have been made possible. Whether or not the quota can be raised to eight bushels or more I do not know. I do not know, either, why the hon. member should have set it at eight bushels rather than moving just one step at a time and suggesting seven bushels.

The house resumed, from Thursday, July 10, consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. Fleming (Eglinton)-Mr. Rea in the chair:
Resolved, that It is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Income Tax Act and to provide, among other things:
1.	That amounts paid after June 17, 1958, for drugs and medicines which have been prescribed by a medical practioner and recorded by a licensed pharmacist be included in the medical expenses that are deductible in computing taxable income.
2.	That amounts paid after June 17, 1958, for eyeglasses, artificial eyes, laboratory or other diagnostic services or transportation to or from a hospital by ambulance be included in the medical expenses that are deductible in computing taxable income.
3.	That for 1958 and subsequent taxation years the maximum amount deductible by corporations for contributions to charitable organizations be increased from 5 per cent of income to 10 per cent of income.
4.	That the rate of interest payable to taxpayers on overpayments of tax for 1958 and subsequent taxation years be increased from 2 per cent to 3 per cent.
5.	That the two year period within which a taxpayer may apply for a refund of an overpayment of tax for a taxation year be increased to four years from the end of the taxation year.
6.	That for 1958 and subsequent taxation years a gift to the spouse of a donor of real property to be used by the donor and the spouse as their home, or a gift to a child of the donor of farm real property to be used in farming operations carried on by the child, or by the child and the donor, shall be exempt from gift tax to the extent of $10,000, provided that no such exemption shall apply more than once during the lifetime of the donor.
7.	That the amount by which any gift tax paid on a gift made within three years prior to death

exceeds any succession duty or estate tax subsequently imposed in respect of a death after June 17, 1958, on that gift under any Act of the Parliament of Canada will be refunded.
8.	That with effect after June 17, 1958, the exemption from the tax on income of non-resident persons now granted in respect of dividends paid by a non-resident-owned investment corporation be changed so as to apply only in respect of dividends paid after the time when the corporation has paid out dividends which in the aggregate equal the undistributed earnings accumulated by the corporation in years when it was not a non-resident-owned investment corporation.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Last night when the committee rose we were discussing paragraph 6 of the resolution. Is the discussion on this paragraph now concluded?

Mr. Chairman, as I am very-interested in the gifts given under a marriage contract, would the minister promise that he will study this matter and consult with his legal advisers with a view to adding something to these provisions so that such gifts may be protected when the bill comes before the house?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I can assure my hon. friend that any suggestion from any part of the house that has merit will certainly be given consideration.

I am not speaking of the principle, I am speaking of the practice. If the minister would bring in an amendment himself we on this side of the house would be very happy.
(Translation):

Mr. Chairman, may I allowed a few remarks with regard to paragraph 6 which has been commented upon by our learned friends in the opposition. According to them, it would seem that in its present form this paragraph would put the province of Quebec in a rather unfavourable position, the provisions of the civil code being what they are.
Two things are, of course, authorized by this paragraph: a tax exemption in respect of a gift made by a husband to his wife, during his own lifetime, of real property to the extent of $10,000, and a further tax exemption in respect of a gift made by a

father to his son of real property to the value of $10,000.
I feel that everybody will agree that this provision is excellent in principle. As for the second part, in particular there is no doubt that it is such as to be of great benefit to our farmers, in so far as it allows the maintenance of the family farm, thus encouraging the father to make a gift to his son in his own lifetime, of the land he farms.
Where the problem becomes somewhat more involved, if my understanding of the first part of the paragraph is correct, is where a gift is made by a husband to his wife.
Every body knows-and our learned friends reminded the house of the fact yesterday-that community property is the general rule in Quebec. This common property is made up of all movable property belonging to the husband and wife before marriage, all movables acquired by them during their marriage, either by gifts or succession, fruits, revenues, interests falling due or received during marriage, and all immovables acquired during marriage.
On the other hand all immovables owned by the consorts on or before the day when the marriage was solemnized, as well as immovables acquired by them, during its continuance, by succession or equivalent process, do not go into the community. Our civil code also provides for a third type of property: property reserved to the wife.
Under the principle of community property, the husband alone has sole control and management of his property and he alone may dispose of it.
As far as any personal property of each spouse, the husband alone administers it but he cannot, without the wife's consent, dispose of any property belonging to her. Finally, there is a third category of property called property reserved to the wife; it is property acquired by the wife as a result of her own savings or use thereof, or resulting from the sale of real estate which she owned. Control and administration of that third category of property rest exclusively with the wife. One point which must not be overlooked is that this institution, community property, gives the wife a half interest in the property. Each spouse has an equal share. Consequently, on the death of the husband, or when in certain cases during marriage, separation of property is declared by the courts, the result is that the wife is entitled to half the community property and
Income Tax Act
her half is not subject to income tax, nor to succession duty tax.
That is one advantage resulting from the principle of separate property. Besides, the matter was referred to yesterday,-and my excellent friend from Hull Mr. Caron recalled it very precisely,-except when ordered by the courts, separate maintenance is instituted by marriage contract which, necessarily, is entered into before marriage. I know that here, in Ontario, this type of contract is entered into after marriage, or at any time during marriage.
The marriage contract can provide for all sorts of conventions, even those which might be void in any other intervivos arrangement. In this way not only can such donations be made in respect of present property but also in respect of future belongings. Those future belongings, if they are set out in the contract, may take effect during the lifetime of the consorts. In this regard I believe that the jurisprudence established by our courts is quite clear. Moreover, Mignault, in his writings on the Quebec Civil Code, volume 6, page 139, clearly expresses that opinion which, in any event, has been abundantly supported by our jurisprudence.
Therefore, nothing stands in the way of taking advantage of this paragraph, since, by way of a marriage contract, a tax exempt gift of $10,000, of real property, for instance, can be made, even though at time of marriage that property may not be at the interested party's disposal, or though he may not have a cent to his name. This real property can be claimed at anytime during the marriage, as long as such a gift has been provided for prior to the marriage and determined by the contract itself.
Obviously, as was rightfully pointed out yesterday, no gift intervivos can be made between husband and wife. They can make no changes in the contractual matrimonial conventions. However, it must be admitted that, when our notaries draw up a contract of separate property, they generally are careful to specify in the contract: a gift in cash or real estate. Through a legal provision under the resolution now being considered, such gift could very well be some real estate worth up to $10,000, which might therefore be exempt from income tax. Of course, the proposed clause under discussion would not affect existing marriage contracts, except where they already provide for such a gift. Therein lies the difficulty. I am

Income Tax Act
sorry that my learned friends in the opposition did not find-and probably for a very good reason-any realistic suggestion by which this paragraph might be adjusted to present conditions in the province of Quebec.
It will be admitted that the principle announced in this paragraph is excellent. It will also be recognized that the second part of the paragraph will be of very great help to the farmers not only of Quebec, but of other provinces as well. Otherwise, I readily admit that the first part of the paragraph will raise some difficulties for the province of Quebec with regard to the provisions of our civil law as they are now.
However, I wonder how it would be possible to amend that paragraph so that it might automatically apply to already existing marriage contracts, unless we encroach upon a field coming exclusively under the jurisdiction of the provinces, and especially of the province of Quebec. We all know to what extent the province of Quebec is jealous, and rightly so, of her institutions and notably of her civil code since, as everyone knows, the settlement of all individual conflicts that might arise, every day as it were, between citizens of the same community, come under the civil code. It is precisely by reason of this vital function that the civil code constitutes the most solid bulwark acquired and preserved by our ethnic group, a bulwark which no doubt has largely contributed to its maintenance and survival.
Under the circumstances, how could the federal parliament compel the province of Quebec to enforce this paragraph without automatically encroaching upon provincial jurisdiction? Unless we simply do away with such an eminently social and familial provision-no one in this house would be in favour of such a solution-there seems to remain but one possible solution, one which lies outside our jurisdiction and comes exclusively under the provincial legislature: i.e., to amend, if it so chooses, section 1265 of the civil code to allow any citizen of that province to take advantage of the clause now under discussion.
This obstacle should not, in my opinion, hamper the work of the federal government. After it has legislated within the limits of its own jurisdiction, it is up to the Quebec provincial government to complete its work and insure its full effect by taking action within its own field and enacting legislation which under the constitution, comes under its exclusive jurisdiction.
Before closing, I must add that for the last few years, a commission in the province of Quebec has been busy redrafting our civil code. I seem to remember, although I [Mr. Dorion.l
could not positively vouch for this, that the Right Hon. Thibodeau Rinfret, chairman of that commission, has indeed observed in the course of interviews given to the press, to the radio and to a group of people concerned, that the problem which we have tackled in connection with section 6 is already being considered: i.e. should we maintain, as a general rule in the province of Quebec, the community property system or should we not substitute for it the separate property system, which is now the exception. In any case, I am convinced that the commission will take note of the amendments made to the Income Tax Act and will definitely endeavour, in the suggestions which it will submit to the government of the province of Quebec, to ensure that all Canadians of the province of Quebec, as well as all Canadians of any other province, may take advantage of that section which, in my opinion, I repeat, seems highly familial and social in its nature.
In view of the fact that, in my opinion, all the steps that the federal government could take to impose upon the province of Quebec the obligation of taking advantage of this section, would constitute an encroachment upon the responsibilities which are exclusively provincial, and it seems to me that we should, under the present conditions, accept this section, leaving the province of Quebec the choice of taking advantage of it by amending the civil code accordingly.

I am very grateful to the member for Bellechasse (Mr. Dorion) for so clearly and accurately outlining the matter. To a person like myself, who has not too much legal knowledge, this was all very interesting but I do not feel quite clear in my mind about one particular matter. As it is, the member for Bellechasse seems to believe that if the federal government were to recognize as gifts between husbands and wives those which are made under a marriage contract, this would be an infringement on provincial jurisdiction. I would appreciate an elaboration on that point.

I am sorry, but what I meant was this. What would be an encroachment, would be to authorize gifts during marriage, in some way or another, if such gifts had not formerly been provided for in the marriage contract. But gifts made under the terms of the marriage contract are altogether different. To my mind advantage may be taken of these gifts mentioned in the marriage contract, even though such gifts be for the future.

In that case, I would ask the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) to

consult with the member for Bellechasse, who could surely be able to inform him in that regard.
(Text):

I was certainly very pleased, Mr. Chairman, to hear the hon. member for Bellechasse present to the committee his studied expose of this situation. It is so typical of him that anything he tackles he does thoroughly and he does well. Certainly there is no difference of opinion on the basic principle which he so clearly enunciated to the committee. There is certainly no difference of opinion on the second half of the resolution, in which we all concur. However, by his presentation the hon. member has just confirmed that in so far as Quebec is concerned, the problem exists. I do not think there is any issue between the opposition and the government on the principle which they are attempting to establish. We are only concerned as to whether or not this principle covers the province of Quebec as clearly and as adequately as it covers the rest of the country.
The presentation by the hon. member for Bellechasse is quite clear. But even so he suggests, and I say this with great respect, that if the legislature of Quebec would amend article 1265 of the civil code the problem would be solved. Since we do not know what the Quebec legislature will do now, when we are debating this legislation, we might not be giving the benefits which are intended by this legislation to the province of Quebec. I was wondering whether we could not suggest an amendment in some form which would cover the situation.
I might say now to the minister that we are seeking to obtain for the husband in Quebec the very same rights which husbands enjoy in the rest of the country; that is our objective. I suggest to the minister that he might consider this form of amendment, because in my humble opinion this is how we might be able to attain our objective under present conditions. I am not moving this as an amendment, but I am merely putting it forward for the minister's consideration. When the time comes this amendment might be made to paragraph 6:
Where the making of a gift as herein contemplated is prohibited by provincial law, but a desire to make such a gift is recorded, there shall be no tax assessable if in the last will and testament of a husband he specifically bequeathes to his wife a legacy, which in effect is similar to the gift as herein contemplated. The deceased's estate shall in that case, for estate taxes, be considered reduced by the amount of the said gift.
I tried to word this as clearly as I could. The intention is that if there is a prohibition in the civil code of Quebec against the making of such gifts, there is no prohibition against
Income Tax Act
the husband making such a gift by will. The husband would have, during his lifetime, declared in writing that he desired to make such a gift but could not do so because of our code. Then if it is later found in his will that he bequeathes to his wife a legacy of $10,000 or less, providing it comes within the framework of being in connection with their home, that $10,000 should not be considered a part of his estate under the new act which we discussed the other day. It may be excluded. If it were declared now that such gift, by legacy, was intended to be a gift under this section, then the intent is clearly expressed and I believe the legal difficulties are surmounted if the federal government will go along and say they will exempt that amount for estate tax.
Later if the legislature of Quebec, as the hon. member for Bellechasse has declared, comes to the aid of husbands in Quebec, I would say tant mieux; then we would have confirmation of it.

At page 2136 of Hansard for yesterday the minister was speaking on this clause 6 of the resolution, and he had this to say:
This provision, which has much to commend it, is available to anybody in Canada once parliament enacts it. If it is my hon. friend's opinion that the law of Quebec prevents some spouses there from deriving benefit from this provision-
The minister was referring to a question put to him by the hon. member for Hull.
-I think in all fairness that should not be pleaded as a reason for denying this benefit to spouses in other provinces-
We on this side of the house quite agree with that, Mr. Chairman. However, I should like to ask the minister whether, in framing the amendment to the act, any consideration was given to the laws of the provinces, and in this instance especially to the laws of Quebec in so far as gifts to spouses are concerned.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, certainly. As a matter of fact this resolution is, in part, designed to give to the spouses in the common law provinces of Canada the benefit that the wife enjoys in Quebec by virtue of the community of property.

I beg to disagree with the minister. 1 do not believe that spouses in Quebec are going to benefit at all from that provision as the law of Quebec stands now, even under community of property or with a separation as to property.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
In the case of marriages in Quebec where community of property exists, if I understand it, the benefit that this particular proposal would create in favour of the wife already exists in the province of Quebec. I think that point has

Income Tax Act
been clearly made. My friend may not agree with it, but I think the point has been clearly established.

I shall try to elucidate this situation in so far as community property is concerned. When a man and woman are married in Quebec-I am referring to those who are now married, not those who may be married in the future-community of property exists if there is no marriage contract signed before the marriage. Then the community property belongs to both at the same time; it is not divided. It is divided only when the death of the husband or wife occurs. Before that, it is administered by the husband alone, without his wife taking any part in the administration of the property.
The exception to this was mentioned by the hon. member for Bellechasse, where property may be reserved to the wife, but that does not enter into our considerations. In so far as community property is concerned, it is not divided before one of the spouses dies; therefore I do not see how they could benefit from this amendment.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have tried to make this point as clear as I could. When my friend says that no benefit will directly accrue to spouses in Quebec under this resolution, what I am submitting to the committee is that in such cases joint ownership already exists under community of property in the province of Quebec.
But does it help in any way? There is the group where the husband and wife have an ante-nuptial contract.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In the case of an ante-nuptial contract you have a different situation, because there the parties can exclude community of property by the terms of the marriage contract.
And do.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes; and in those cases, as I understand it, it will be competent for them to make gifts. After the very clear exposition of this matter by the hon. member for Bellechasse I would have thought the point had been clarified. There has been a useful discussion. It seems to me the point has been established reasonably clearly now.
I can assure hon. members, Mr. Chairman, that this matter was very carefully canvassed from all aspects. All hon. members are aware that in the province of Quebec, in cases where community of property does exist, the wife has already, by the fact of the marriage, acquired a joint ownership in the property of the husband. Consequently she already enjoys the benefit that this legislation is intended to make it possible for the 
parties to a marriage in other provinces to create in favour of the wife in respect of their home, and as well for the benefit of those parties to marriages in the province of Quebec who have, by ante-nuptial contracts, excluded the principle of community of property.

I should like to clear up one point for the minister, if I can. The minister is under the impression that where there is community of property, the wife already has what is rightfully hers, halfinterest in the property. But that is not quite the case. Even where there is community of property the husband and wife can have property of their own. There are certain things which husbands and wives have which do not fall into the community. One of these is property which they inherit.
For example, if a husband inherits the home in which he resides, that is the husband's property. The maintenance of the home is the community obligation, but that property is the husband's and he can do away with it by will if he wishes. The wife has no interest in that. I hope the minister sees the difference under those circumstances. If a husband has property which is exclusively his own and which does not fall into the community, or within that property which we are talking about, why should not the husband who has his own property which does not form part of the community not be able to give away part of that property and make a gift to his wife of $10,000? Under our present law he cannot give his own personal property, not the community property; he cannot give that to the wife.
There is a material and serious difference there, I submit to the minister, and that is the butt of our entire discussion of this whole thing. It is with reference to that $10,000 of the husband's own estate which he is prevented from giving to his wife under our law. The law as contemplated here intends that to be the case but it cannot be the case in the province of Quebec. A husband cannot even give his own personal property to his wife if he wants to do so, if they live under the regime of community as to property. It is that difficulty which we are trying to remedy in order to give that husband the privilege not of giving community property but of giving his own property which does not form part of the community.
That is the basic difference. If the minister will look at the matter I am sure he will understand it perhaps in another light. I understand certainly that the hon. member for Bellechasse gave an excellent expose and a complete review of the situation in the province of Quebec. But even so he left a

doubt, and he would call upon the legislature of Quebec to make it possible to give effect to the law which we are now attempting to pass in this house. I am all in favour of that law, but I am apprehensive that it might not be possible for the matter to be dealt with in the province of Quebec as effectively as we should like to see it done.

I should like to add a word or two, Mr. Chairman. I think the hon. member for Cartier must realize this, and I should like to say this for some other people in the house who perhaps have had more experience in the common law than in the civil law. If we are dealing with article 1265 in the province of Quebec I think he must admit that it is perhaps one article that has had more jurisprudence on it, even within our own province, than most other articles. I think he is doing a little bit of crystal-ball gazing and is prejudging the situation a little bit.
After the clarification by the hon. member for Bellechasse I feel that we should get on with this thing. Even in the province of Quebec I say we have a great deal of jurisprudence on this very point. I can quite easily visualize, especially on the federal level, this debate going on for weeks and weeks. I repeat I think he is prejudging the situation. After the remarks made by the hon. member for Bellechasse I can quite easily see this matter being straightened out in the near future. In view of that possibility I hope hon. members might consider these remarks.
I am in the position of a juryman in this case, because I know nothing about the Quebec law except what I have listened to here this morning.
Jurymen do not decide on the law.

In listening to the arguments that have been put forward on both sides of the house, and especially those by the minister himself, it seems to me that everybody is overlooking the real principle in this clause. The real principle is not security of the family-something which the minister stressed-which he is giving to provinces other than Quebec but which is already enjoyed in Quebec; and it is not the fact that some people in Quebec cannot make gifts unless they separate their property before marriage. The real principle is surely tax relief. This measure is designed to give a certain amount of relief to taxpayers. That is all it is for. We are giving an exemption for tax purposes in a case of this kind. Surely we must keep to the main principle and treat all taxpayers alike. If we are not treating

certain taxpayers in Quebec in the same way as we are treating taxpayers in other parts of Canada, then we should take some other measure to try to bring about that result.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I should like to make two brief observations on the remarks just delivered by the hon. member for St. Denis.
In the first place, this resolution and the bill to follow will do all the federal jurisdiction can do to extend this benefit to everybody in Canada, regardless of the province in which he or she lives. The federal government can do no more than legislate for the benefit of all, and that is what this legislation will do. I do not think, notwithstanding all the repetitive arguments to which we have been listening, that it can be contended, as my hon. friend assumes, that there is going to be any portion of this benefit denied to those who live in the province of Quebec, and I simply refer him to the exposition on this subject delivered this morning by a brilliant advocate of the province of Quebec in the person of the hon. member for Bellechasse.
On the second point, my hon. friend complains that in the case of gifts from parent to son the benefit of exemption should not be confined to those cases where the gift is that of a farm. This resolution has been deliberately drawn in this form because of the desire to keep the sons of farmers on the farms, and because so many of these questions arise with respect to property located in rural areas. This is a situation which occurs over and over again in all parts of the country and has given rise to this particular amendment.
I do ask the committee to recall that we had a very extended discussion on this subject, and I think it is clearly understood that we are trying to bring forward two new types of alleviation of the tax burden. Most of the hon. members who have been speaking in this house this morning and who spoke last night have been here for a long time, but at no time have they brought forward such suggestions as those for which they are so strongly arguing this morning. The need has existed all this time, if there is any such need at all, but I do ask hon. members to weigh 57071-3-136J
Income Tax Act
well the fact that in this paragraph are attempts to bring relief, and I think very useful relief, to all parts of Canada.
First, this alleviation is with respect to a gift by one spouse to the other of an interest in the home; we are here proposing that up to the amount of $10,000 that gift should be free of tax. This means, with the present exemption on gifts between spouses of $4,000 per year, we have now created a means by which the wife can be secure in the ownership of the home of the couple in all parts of Canada. Second, in the case of a young man on a farm, the father can now convey to the son, up to the amount for which provision has been made, an interest in that farm which will have the effect of keeping such a young man on the farm and will, we think, contribute not only to the easing of the tax burden but will serve the socially desirable need to maintain agricultural production and retain the ownership of these farms in those families where it is clearly to the national advantage to do so.

I think the practice of having joint tenancies with respect to the resident's property has been growing in volume in recent years, and I want to know whether or not it is intended, as referred to in this section, that the bill should provide that only joint tenancies created since 1958 will avoid gift tax.

Mr. Chairman, may I say to fellow hon. members of this house from the province of Quebec, through you, sir, that those of us who are new members and perhaps particularly those who are new members from the west have been extremely interested in the discussion that occurred this morning and last evening. Since coming to this house on May 12 we have heard frequent reference to one word in particular on the part of hon. gentlemen from Quebec. It is one of the very few French words that I have had time to learn. I refer to the word "unity". Certainly if we are to attain unity in this country we need to know more and more about the problems of the various sections of the nation. Speaking for myself I have gained a new conception of at least one problem in the province of Quebec and it is for that reason that I ask the indulgence of the house for a few moments while I endeavour to explain, as best I may, the relationship of this particular paragraph to the people of the prairies.
Let me say at once that we believe this represents an admirable amendment to the Income Tax Act, one that has long been needed. I say that for this reason. Our part of Canada, unlike the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, has been more recently settled. The people who live there are to a large degree the original pioneer settlers. Many are reaching the age where death is taking its toll and disability is rendering many of them unable to work any longer.
I am not a member of the bar but I have had a rather extensive experience with farm people both as a technical agriculturist and as a businessman. We have, as the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River has indicated, adopted the practice of joint tenancies in that part of the country and we have found that the principle of joint tenancy is becoming more and more popular. I would not say that at this moment it was widespread throughout the part of the country from which I come, but certainly it is being viewed with a great deal more favour than it was a few years ago.
With respect to a joint tenancy in Alberta, should the husband die within a few years of the establishment of the joint tenancy the widow is required by the income tax branch to establish the validity of her claim under the joint tenancy. In many cases, of course, this is impossible. Frequently she is unable to produce any evidence that she has an actual
Income Tax Act
financial right in the property and as a result taxation is applied and the widow is at some disadvantage.
It seems to us as laymen, that women in our part of the country-this question is frequently discussed there-I feel I can say this since the election of March 31 is now over and I cannot be accused of a motive- and particularly the pioneer women have never been fully recognized at law. This is a strange situation because the wife and daughter have played an equal part to that played by the husband and son in the development of that part of the country. Certainly these women have done their full part m developing western Canada. We appreciate this amendment for the very valid reason that to some degree at least it gives to the women of our part of the country, regardless of what may be the situation elsewhere, recognition at law and a right to which they have been long entitled.
Let me add that what is true of the wife and the widow is also true of the working son and the fatherless son. Did I wish to take the time I could cite a number of instances where a young man has worked with his father from boyhood into early manhood and yet at the time of his father's death he has had no equity in the farm which he has helped to build up. From the point of view of those of us who have to some degree studied this problem on the prairies and from that point of view of those of us who have had contact with actual cases, we believe the amendment is to be commended and we wholeheartedly endorse it.

Mr. Chairman, may I say first of all that I greatly appreciate the introductory remarks of the hon. member for Medicine Hat. I believe they were in themselves a valuable contribution to our national unity. We were pleased to hear the hon. member explain the interest he has in the problem we are trying to raise with respect to the province of Quebec and that he is anxious to acquaint himself with our problems. Hon. members from the province of Quebec feel that the question we are seeking to raise at this time is one of considerable importance to us. I think it would be regrettable if an important aspect of this piece of legislation were to go through, leaving behind it some misunderstandings as to its exact meaning. I agree, and hon. members on this side of the house have agreed from the beginning, that this is highly useful legislation applicable throughout the country in most of its aspects but with respect to one particular aspect there is some doubt as to its application in the province of Quebec.
I listened with interest to the hon. member for Bellechasse in his very learned, fair and

Income Tax Act
complete expose of the civil code relative to this matter. The minister has asked us to refer to the remarks made by the hon. member for Bellechasse and I think he will recall that the hon. member for Bellechasse said there was only one part of this section which was not necessarily applicable to the province of Quebec. He made the point that we, as the federal government, could not legislate in order to force the provincial government to modify its civil code with which I fully agree, but I believe it would be possible for the federal government to slightly amend the wording of this clause in order to eliminate what I believe is a discrimination affecting some of the people in that province under this important legislation.
I am not going into the problem of the community of property; I think the hon. member for Bellechasse has explained that quite well. I believe that the part that deals with those people who are married, and there is separation of property, is the nub of this whole problem. I would like to clear up the matter in my own mind by asking the minister whether or not it would be applicable to those people. For instance, take the case of a couple who enter into a contract prior to marriage in which the spouse makes a gift of, let us say, $10,000 in real property to his wife to be payable during the course of marriage. Would this gift be exempted or not; would he be able to benefit from this section of the act?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I answered that question last night, Mr. Chairman. I was asked if a donation in cash would qualify and I answered no; it must be a donation of an interest in real property which is to constitute the joint home of the spouse and the donor.
Am I to understand that a contract that was entered into by two people before marriage in which there was a gift of real property would be exempt from taxes even though-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No; my hon. friend is asking me about the position of a gift of money, or successive gifts of money. These are recognized at the present time as gifts. The act exempts gifts up to $4,000 per annum. This new exemption is in addition to that. This applies to a gift of real property, or an interest in real property, which constitutes the home of the spouse and donor, and it applies in the case of a gift to the spouse by the donor; if the gift takes effect on the marriage, then it will qualify. If it is something that preceded the marriage and the parties were not at that time in the relationship of spouses, then it could not be expected to qualify.
That is exactly the point. We have this problem in the province of Quebec. In order to be able to make a gift it has to be done before marriage.
A contract has to be entered into before marriage.

The contract has to be entered into before marriage. It seems to me relatively simple for the government to include those particular circumstances by way of amendment in order that these people who are in separation as to property might be able to qualify, would it not?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If the gift takes effect at the time the parties become spouses, then obviously it will qualify under this clause. As I understand it, the contract is entered into on what is a provisional or a conditional basis, the condition being that it shall not come into effect unless and until the parties wed. If the gift of real property or an interest in real property takes effect on the marriage, then-
Or after.

Then, the answer is in the affirmative.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, if the gift takes effect on the marriage then at that moment the parties are in the relationship of spouses and I think the gift comes within the terms of the clause.

On the same subject, I understand that people from Quebec who are married or thereafter get married and include in their marriage contract, where there is separation as to property, a gift of real property to a spouse, will benefit from this clause. What about those people who are now married and who did include, let us say, 10 years ago, a donation of $10,000 of real property, the donation to take effect tomorrow, would they benefit tomorrow?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, for all persons in all provinces in all parts of Canada this provision will extend the exemption in the case of such gifts occurring on or after January 1, 1958.

I should like to direct the minister's attention to another problem. The minister in referring to the second part of this section speaks about a gift from father to son. The section makes no reference at all to a father or even a mother; it speaks of a spouse and a donor.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It speaks of a child of the donor.

That is right; the donor can be the mother or the father. That is the point I am trying to make. The hon. member for Medicine Hat spoke quite properly about the rights to which women in his part of the country are perhaps entitled. Among other things is the right to make such a gift by a donor within the meaning of section 6. I draw to the minister's attention the fact that women in Quebec, common as to property, cannot be donors of immovable property. Therefore, here again the women of Quebec are unintentionally being discriminated against while women in other parts of the country can donate to their children. Women in the province of Quebec cannot, if they are common as to property, be donors because the husband has the administration not only of the community property but also of his wife's property. Perhaps the thing should be looked at again and if possible give the women of Quebec the same right.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If there is any discrimination it is not created by this provision; indeed, it is not created by any federal legislation. We cannot remove any discrimination, if discrimination has been imposed, under the law of the province of Quebec. This is taxing legislation. We have made it universal in its application in all parts of Canada. It is fair, it is equitable legislation. There is no discrimination created by this legislation and there is nothing that we can do about that situation which my hon. friend mentioned.

There is no doubt that what the minister says is perfectly correct; the legislation is not discriminatory and has not that intention. That is perfectly true. But its end result in so far as a section of this country is concerned is that it is indirectly a discrimination. It is on that that we should like to get a legal opinion. In other words, we are prepared to give something to the citizens of the country, and yet in a certain part of the country they are not able to take advantage of it and that in itself, although the legislation is not discriminatory, is a form of discrimination.

friend suggest that the hands of parliament must be tied and that this kind of alleviation should be denied to persons elsewhere? We are creating no discrimination. So far as parliament can do it, this is given to all.

not be ultra vires. Is that not the whole point? We have spent about three hours on it now.

In western Canada we certainly go along with it because in Alberta we have a Torrens land titles system in which there is joint title. speechtext: Shall we continue with discussion of clause 8?

I believe that this is one of those loophole corrections which probably does not affect a great many taxpayers. Am I right in thinking that under the present law if a company is, and always has been, what is known as an n.r.o. company, the dividends paid by it are exempt from withholding tax?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is correct, Mr. Chairman. This is to meet that situation, where a company that has not been a nonresident investment corporation but is turned into one; if an effort were made in that direction, it could take advantage of two exemptions that exist at the present time where there should be only one.
The proposed amendment does not affect the situation that I described?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No, the proposed amendment will permit one exemption, and properly so, but not the two. The house may be interested in the meaning of this. These non-resident investment corporations are corporations of which the shareholders reside outside of Canada. The n.r.o. company is subject to a tax of 15 per cent each year on its income from all sources, but is exempt from the 15 per cent tax normally paid on dividends by Canadian corporations to non-resident shareholders.
Now, if non-residents invested directly in shares of a Canadian company or in Canadian bonds they would pay to Canada only the 15 per cent non-resident tax on their dividends or interest. But if these non-residents formed an n.r.o. holding company to hold their investments in Canada, they still pay

Supply-Agriculture
only the 15 per cent tax in Canada on their income from their investment. But for certainty of collection, it is paid each year by the n.r.o. instead of when actually withdrawn from the country in the form of dividends. Now, that is the present situation.
This is the loophole that could occur under existing law. Where a company in Canada was acquired by non-residents, and which was carrying on an active business and was not up to that time an n.r.o., and then became an n.r.o. it might have undistributed income accumulated while it was an ordinary company which it could now pay out as dividends to its shareholders since dividends from n.r.o.'s are free from non-resident tax. This resolution proposes that this loophole be plugged by providing that dividends from mr.o.'s shall not be exempt from non-resident tax until all the income accumulated while the corporation was previously not an n.r.o. has been paid out.
