1. Departmental administration, including advisory committee on agricultural services, $674,164.

When the estimates of the Department of Agriculture were briefly before the house on Wednesday afternoon I had been giving a brief summary of some of the changes that had taken place during the past year so far as agriculture is concerned, as well as a brief outline of the agricultural situation as it appears now. I had been dealing with these matters in a general way and had dealt with some of the more important agricultural products such as wheat and cattle.
I had made reference to the amount of beef exported during the past year.
I should like now to continue with those remarks and say something about the prices received for a few of our other major agricultural products. In 1957, the price of good steers at Toronto averaged $19.05 per hundred pounds live weight, 25 cents higher than in 1956. The average price of all cattle marketed was $16.10, almost the same as the $16.05 average in 1956. The strong domestic demand for cattle-
Was that $16.25? [Mr. Fleming (Eglinton)J

No, the average price of all cattle was $16.10 and in 1956 it was $16.05, almost the same.
The strong domestic demand for cattle, in conjunction with the heavy United States demand that developed in the last part of
1957,	resulted in a substantial increase in cattle prices between October 1957 and April
1958.	Good steers at Toronto averaged $22.26 per hundred pounds in March, 1958 compared with $18.78 the year previously, an increase of upward of four cents a pound. The high level of marketings and the strong demand was reflected in the total value of commercial marketings, being $116 million in the first quarter of 1958 compared with $69 million in the corresponding period of 1957. The gain in cattle prices has been responsible to quite a considerable extent for the fact that the total cash income of farmers during the first quarter of 1958 is considerably greater than in the first quarter of 1956 or 1957.
The figures are given in the dominion bureau of statistics farm cash income publication, and they show that in the first quarter, that is January to March of 1958, farm cash income was $618 million, which is up $42 million from the $576 million of a year earlier. I think that we have been very fortunate, so far as our cattle prices are concerned during these past nine months in particular, in the fact that we had increased numbers of cattle available to market at these higher prices.
After cattle the most important meat production which we have is hogs and I should like to say just a few words about that matter. At June 1, 1957 hogs on farms numbered 4.9 million, only slightly more than the 4.7 million at June 1, 1956. In 1957, 5.4 million hogs were slaughtered and graded in federally inspected and approved plants, 9 per cent less than in 1956. The retention of hogs for breeding indicated by the drop in output in 1957, in spite of the large number on farms, is reflected in the current and anticipated increase in marketings during the present year. In other words, although there were more hogs on farms in 1957, there were fewer slaughtered than in the previous year, which indicated a considerable number was retained for breeding purposes which means that we shall have a much larger flow this year and in the early part of 1959.
Gradings in the first three months of 1958 were 1,542,000, 7 per cent higher than in 1957 In other words, this increased movement of hogs to market is already showing up in the first quarter of 1958. That increase has been mainly on the prairies. The amount of increase in hog production in the eastern part of the country has not been very great but in the prairies it has been very marked.

Per capita consumption of pork was 46.2 pounds in 1957, 6.7 per cent more than in 1956. In the first quarter of 1958 a further increase in consumption is indicated. Domestic disappearance from commercial marketings totalled 177 million pounds in that quarter, a rise of 9 per cent over 1957. In other words, although we have more hogs now coming to market, the market has been able to absorb those. The consumption has increased.
The equivalent of 322,000 hogs were exported as pork products in 1957. Exports amounted to 6 per cent of total commercial marketings in 1957 as compared with 9 per cent of the total in 1956. In other words, we were able to consume sufficiently more at home so that we had a lesser amount available for export.
In the first quarter of 1958 exports were 14.5 million pounds compared with 11.3 million pounds a year earlier. In other words, exports are going ahead. They have gone ahead again in this first quarter of 1958.
Grade A hogs at Toronto averaged $31.05 per hundred pounds dressed weight during the first quarter. That is exclusive of the federal government premium of $2 per head. In 1956 the average price was $27.50 and the ten-year average-that is from 1948 to 1957- was $29.68, which means that the price of hogs has been relatively quite high during this last year of 1957. The estimated value of hogs marketed and inspected in approved packing plants was $65.9 million in the first quarter of 1958 and $66.3 million in the same period of 1957 or approximately the same.
The production of sheep and lambs is one branch of agriculture in which we are deficient.

I was just saying, Mr. Chairman, that as far as the production of sheep is concerned, Canada is quite deficient. We import the great bulk of the wool which we use and we import quite a large number of the lambs and sheep which we eat. The national flock numbered 1.7 million at June 1, 1957, only slightly more than at the same period of 1956. The 1957 total was only about half the pre-war numbers and the prewar numbers were less than they had been in the earlier period. In other words, we have had a marked decline during the past 20 to 25 years in sheep production in Canada.

Supply-Agriculture
The stabilized price which was put into effect for wool at 60 cents a pound was intended to act as an incentive to sheep producers, to encourage them to stay in the sheep business and to encourage them to increase their flocks because this is one branch of agriculture which we need to encourage. We are certainly not threatened with any surplus as far as it is concerned. Sheep, of course, are a type of livestock which can be used profitably on very poor land which will not profitably support cattle and other types of livestock. The import of mutton and lamb -and it was mainly lamb-amounted to 12.3 million pounds in 1957, which was 19 per cent more than in 1956 and about half the output of the Canadian product from inspected plants. It is the intention, of course, that we could and should increase our sheep production in order to meet our local needs. Practically the entire amount imported originated in New Zealand and Australia.
In the first quarter of the present year prices for lambs averaged higher than in 1957, largely owing to the influence of prices of competing meats. In March of 1958 good lambs at Toronto averaged $24.44 per 100 pounds compared with $22.37 a year ago.
Next I should like to say something about the dairying industry. Dairying is a branch of agriculture in which more farmers have some interest and from which they derive part of their revenue than is the case in any other branch of the agriculture industry. The great majority of farmers in Canada keep at least a few cows. It is therefore an industry of extreme importance to the entire agriculture picture.
Milk production in 1957 was 17.3 billion pounds, only slightly above that of 1956. Since mid-1957 production in each month has exceeded output in the corresponding period of the preceding year. This, of course, is undoubtedly due to better prices as far as most milk products are concerned.
Production during the first quarter of 1958 exceeded that of the preceding year by about 300 million pounds, an increase of 10 per cent. That is quite a marked increase in the amount of milk produced in the first quarter of 1958 as compared with the first quarter of 1957. This year the bulk of the additional milk has gone into the production of creamery butter. Production of this commodity in 1957 of 303 million pounds was about the same as in 1956. Domestic disappearance, which showed an increase in the early months, began to decline around October, 1957. This decrease has continued into the present year. However, in spite of the drop in domestic disappearance stocks were reduced and at the

Supply-Agriculture
end of 1957 totalled 69.9 million pounds compared with 88.2 million pounds at the beginning of the year.
Prices of butter remained stable at approximately the support level during the first seven months of 1957, and then strengthened because there were some indications of the possibility of a tight supply position early in 1958. As a matter of fact, shortly after taking over as Minister of Agriculture, I found that the butter trade and the officials in the department were quite fearful that we would have a definite shortage of butter and be forced into the position of having to import butter into the country.
This was said by the previous minister.

It therefore seemed obvious that some measure was necessary in order to encourage the putting of whole milk into butter rather than into cheese and other products and of course action was taken in order to increase butter prices and this had the object of diverting considerable amounts of milk from cheese and other types of production into butter so that we now have ample supplies of butter.
Production in the last few months of the year rose well above year-earlier levels and prices continued fairly stable at the higher level. Current receipts at Montreal-this is not in new boxes as we buy it in the agricultural stabilization board but in used fibre boxes-were quoted at 57-57J cents per pound at mid-July, 1957 and were 62 cents per pound in December.
Output of butter in the first three months of 1958 continued at the high level of late 1957, and production was 8.6 million pounds more than a year previously. At the same time consumption continued below the preceding year's level and was 2.8 million pounds less in the first three months of 1958 than in the same period of 1957.
Stocks of butter at May 1, 1958-that is, a little more than a month ago-at the beginning of the 1958-59 dairy year, amounted to 35.2 million pounds compared with 36.9 million pounds at that date in 1957.
From this I think it is clear that the stocks are about the same as they were a year ago, and bearing in mind the fact that consumption is down a little while production is up, we are sure of ample stocks for the balance of this dairy year, that is to say, up until next May. The prices of butter have remained steady in the last few months and have averaged 62f cents per pound in the last week of March, 1958 as compared with 58 cents per pound a year ago.

Cheddar cheese production in 1957 was 95.6 million pounds and so was substantially higher than in the preceding several years and exceeded production of 1956 by 12.8 per cent. The year 1957 was a big year so far as cheese production was concerned; that is, as far as recent years go, because during the first world war and prior thereto we produced a great deal more cheese than we do today. In the first quarter of 1958 output dropped to the normal level over recent years of 7.4 million pounds but manufacture in that period was considerably more than in the year previous. Exports dropped sharply in 1957, the 8.1 million pounds exported being 3.4 million pounds less than in 1956 and 5.3 million pounds less than in 1955.
This decrease in exports of cheese, of course, is due to the high price at which our cheese sells on the United Kingdom market compared with the prices paid for Australian and New Zealand cheese, which sell there at around 16 to 18 cents per pound or less than half at which our cheese sells, namely approximately 40 cents per pound. We have therefore a very limited market for our cheese. The domestic market accounted for 75.2 million pounds of cheese in 1957 compared with 72 million pounds in 1956. With the sharp upturn in production and the reduction in exports, stocks in storage were built up during the year and at the end of December, 1957 they amounted to 52 million pounds as against 39.6 million pounds in the previous year. Domestic consumption in the first three months of 1958 was approximately normal, the relatively large stocks at the end of March of 41.2 million pounds reflecting last year's heavy production and accumulation in storage.
Cheese prices were strong early in 1957 but eased as a result of the high level of production accumulated in storage. During March, 1957 prices at factory in Ontario were about 34 cents per pound and at year end were approximately 32 cents per pound. The prices in the first quarter of 1958 have fluctuated within a narrow range and were 34 to 34J cents per pound during March. The increase in price has been due, of course, to the price having been stabilized at 34 cents in Ontario and 33 J cents at Montreal.
Dry skimmed milk, which is the final dairy product on which I wish to say a word, has been one of the most difficult products for us to handle and dispose of. Domestic disappearance rose during the year, but at a lower rate than production. Since exports accounted for only 719,000 pounds during the year there was a considerable accumulation of powder in storage and as the situation developed import controls were applied in order to prevent

the great influx of dry skimmed milk from all countries of the world, which had been going on during the early part of 1957.
Output of dry skimmed milk continued at a high level in the first quarter of 1958 and at the end of March this year totalled 19.6 million pounds, roughly double the 9.5 million pounds produced in the same period of 1957. The extreme difficulty in disposing of this dry skimmed milk either in Canada or overseas made it necessary to reduce the support price which, it was quite evident, had acted as an incentive price and had resulted in a considerable increase in the number of dry skimmed milk plants and in the first three months of this year, as I have said, had doubled production compared with the previous year.
At May 1, 1958 there were about 40 million pounds of this product in storage, compared with about 5 million pounds at May 1, 1957. The recently announced stabilization price of 15 cents per pound for spray process powder and 64 cents a pound for creamery butter mean that last year's price relationships in terms of milk will be roughly maintained. In other words, the return to farmers for their marketing will be roughly the same this year as it was during the last three or four months during 1957.
I have a lot of notes in regard to other products such as apples, potatoes, fowl, eggs and so on, but I do not think I had better take the time of the house to go into these matters at this time. Undoubtedly questions will be asked on these matters and we will deal with them as they come up during the course of the estimates.
I would, however, like to say something about the research activities of the department. I think we have concentrated a great deal too much on the question of prices during recent years with respect to agricultural matters. Most of the discussions in this house for a great many years have been concerned with the prices of agricultural products and very little attention has been paid to the scientific activities carried on in order to improve the yields of many such products and to eliminate the diseases which cut down those yields. Actually, the activities of the research scientists have contributed a very great deal to farmers' incomes during the past several years and I think it is quite apparent that the introduction of Marquis wheat and latterly Selkirk wheat has improved farm incomes to a considerable extent. Many other improvements have been brought about and it will be possible to bring about many further improvements. In many cases the results of the research in the agricultural field have actually increased yield, two, three, four, five or more than five times. Such increases in yield have, of course, meant a greater return to the 57071-3-137J
Supply-Agriculture
farmer, and are more important than a great many of the things about which we have heard so much, such as trying to improve market facilities, to secure very high prices for particular products and to keep price supports under them and many other things along that line. I think we have neglected our research scientists and the wonderful work they are doing in our discussions on the agricultural estimates.
I would like therefore to briefly indicate some of the activity carried on in this respect over the last few years and to tell the house of some of the advances made to illustrate the great contribution these men are making to agriculture. Firstly, may I mention the Lacombe bacon hog. This particular breed, developed at Lacombe, was released to the public in October, 1957 by the Canada-wide distribution of 50 Lacombe boars. Crosses between the Lacombe and Yorkshire exhibit hybrid vigour for growth and they are at least equal to the parental breeds in respect to quality. We have high hopes that this new breed will improve grading and will also enable hogs to go to market earlier. This will of course mean that the farmers will be able to make considerably more profit from them.
A team of biochemists and physiologists has joined the animal husbandman in an intensive search for the factors causing urinary calculi in range cattle. A breakthrough should provide information of great practical value in controlling the problem.
There have been some interesting experiments on pasture. At Nappan, Nova Scotia, an average gain of 548 pounds per acre of beef was secured on fertilized dikeland pasture as compared with 445 pounds on fertilized upland pasture. Corresponding gains on unfertilized pasture were 363 pounds and 233 pounds per acre, respectively. This work is of considerable importance, particularly in the maritime provinces, because we are reclaiming quite large areas down there through the activities of the Maritime Marshland Rehabilitation Act and I think this reclaimed marshland provided the basis upon which a very thriving beef industry can be built up in the maritime provinces, placing the agriculture of those provinces upon a much sounder basis than for many years past.
Cattle warbles have proved a troublesome problem and do great damage to our leather production. Work is progressing favourably on new chemical control methods that destroy cattle grubs before they reach the animals' backs and damage their hides. This promises a distinct advance on previous measures which kill the grubs after they have completed their migration through the body. However, much work remains to be done in

evaluating the total effects of this type of treatment and new materials are under constant test.
The department has an all-out program designed to protect and improve the wheat of the future from both genetic and quality standpoints. Varieties are being developed to meet all foreseen eventualities. Increased emphasis is being placed on superior quality in the new lines. Selkirk, rust resistant, and Chinook, wheat stem sawfly-resistant, are examples of contributions.
The department has released a new malting barley, Parkland, by name, which is at least equal to existing varieties in quality, and superior in agronomic characteristics. It is outyielding Montcalm by seven to ten bushels per acre and has much better lodging resistance.
Cumino sweet clover is another development. The use of this new variety, developed in our laboratories at Saskatoon, will remove the danger of sweet clover poisoning of livestock, and will eliminate melilot taint resulting from volunteer sweet clover in wheat fields. It is the first coumarin-free variety of white blossom sweet clover which has been made available to agriculture.
For the first time in the history of Canadian agriculture a hardy variety of perennial rye grass, capable of surviving winter throughout large areas in eastern Canada, as well as in British Columbia, has been made available in 1957. This variety, known as the Norlea, was developed at Ottawa as a result of 17 years of breeding work. That gives you some idea of the amount of time required in order to develop new varieties and, in other cases, to eliminate certain types of disease and things of that kind.
Rambler alfalfa was developed at Swift Current and licensed in 1955. It is a creeping-rooted, drought resistant variety suitable for dryland pasture.
Annual surveys provide advance information on impending outbreaks of insect pests and enable provincial governments and growers to take proper precautionary measures. This service has contributed greatly to reduced losses from such occurrences as the white grub outbreak of 1957 in Ontario and Quebec, the constantly shifting hazard of the spruce budworm throughout eastern Canada, and the present grasshopper menace that threatens the prairies. A selective spray program has been developed in Nova Scotia against the codling moth and other fruit tree pests. In this program chemicals are selected that also allow control by the natural enemies of the pests involved. This has resulted in a reduction in costs of spray materials from $50 per acre, in comparable areas of eastern

United States where this method is not used, to $4.80 per acre, as revealed by independent economic studies. This saving is very important to the established method of production and the type of market available to growers in Nova Scotia, and is a good example of what I said at the beginning regarding the way in which the efforts of our research scientists in agriculture can and do improve the return that farmers get from their crops.
There are several other examples which, perhaps, I will not take time to deal with; various types of experiments, all of which are interesting. I think, perhaps, that I should refer to one or two more. One concerns strawberries. Four new varieties, Cavalier, Grenadier, Guardsman and Redcoat have been introduced from Ottawa. I do not know why those names were considered particularly appropriate for strawberries coming from Ottawa, but perhaps they are. These varieties should have wide adaptation in the east as well as possibilities on the west coast. Cavalier is an early variety, while Guardsman may have a special place as a late ripening variety.
Reliable methods for testing the cold resistance of fruit tree seedlings are being developed. If this program is successful it should practically eliminate the present severe losses from winter killing.
Summerland experimental farm is cooperating with industry in evaluating the 25-bushel containers for handling apples and introducing them to growers; what is known as bulk handling. These are expected to reduce capital outlay for containers and labour handling costs, something which is essential in the fruit industry if growers are to receive an adequate return.
Even Newfoundland has not been neglected in these researches. The peat bogs of Newfoundland have received considerable attention. Agricultural engineers and agronomists are studying methods of drainage and fertility requirements. There have been marked yield increases from applications of both nitrogen and phosphorus on newly drained and limed bogs.
A good deal of work has been done with regard to irrigation as well as drainage, and agrometeorologists and agronomists working together are evolving formulae regulating irrigation to a schedule which permits optimum growth of crops, protects the soil, and economizes in the use of water.
Mr. Chairman, these are only a few of the numerous scientific studies which are going on, and each of them which comes to successful fruition is, of course, extremely helpful to agriculture and, taken together,

these studies do a great deal to improve the general economic position of farmers.
Just before I close I should like to pay tribute to the employees of the Department of Agriculture. I have found them extremely competent and co-operative; I have found that they are deeply interested in agriculture and in the people engaged in agriculture, and they are undoubtedly making a great contribution to this, our most important basic industry.

Mr. Chairman, at the beginning of my remarks I want to say to my good friend the Minister of Agriculture that I am in 100 per cent agreement with him with regard to what he said in the last part of his speech about the employees of the Department of Agriculture. I have dealt with them on many occasions over 30 years and found them very loyal. They have done great work for the Canadian farmers, as a whole, in this country.
Secondly, I am 100 per cent in agreement with the minister in what he is doing about raising the standards of animals and produce of every kind produced on the farms. Over 30 or 35 years I have noticed that there has been an improvement in every way of working the land so as to produce better crops and raise finer animals. This improvement is due to the fine work that has been done by federal and provincial representatives of agriculture.
As I said at the beginning of my remarks I wish to make known to hon. members the situation in my riding. There are very many new members and unfortunately for the good of the Canadian people too many of them are Tory. However, those new members I have met since the beginning of the session have been very nice people but, as I said, far too many of them sit on the wrong side of the house and do not advocate a good policy.
The riding of Russell has a population of about 96,000 of whom approximately 32,000 live in the rural districts. Many of those live in small villages and towns; perhaps 8,000 in all. Therefore only about 24,000 of my constituents are real farmers. I want to tell you that I have the best farmers that one can find in this country. Most of them are engaged in mixed farming. They raise every kind of cattle. Some raise chickens and there are many garden farmers who grow the vegetables and fruits to supply the city of Ottawa and surrounding territory. It is not uncommon in Russell to see a farmer milking more than 40 cows a day. Many raise from between 100 and 300 pigs each year. Many raise over 40,000 chickens annually. The farmers there work very hard but, as the
Supply-Agriculture
minister pointed out, they could improve a great deal in their methods of operation. In many cases they could derive twice the revenue from their farms and their operations in cattle and chicken raising than they are now getting.
I want to draw to the attention of new members the agricultural picture in my riding. I need not do this for the older members many of whom I have known for 12 years and so we are good friends. I am interested in the farmer but not for political reasons because less than one-quarter of the electorate in my riding engages in farming.
I am interested in the farmer because I have some knowledge of farming. I was one of a family of 13 born on a farm. I have had business dealings with farmers for 40 years as well as with labourers and people in every conceivable occupation in cities and towns.
I have been dealing not only with farmers but with labourers and business people in Casselman for 35 years. I had over 1,000 acres of good farm land under cultivation and was responsible-although not personally -for the milking of between 75 to 80 cows.
While I am referring to Casselman I wish to point out to the Minister of Agriculture that we had a nice plant there dealing with flax and linen. It had up to 4,000 acres under flax. This brought good money to the labourers and farmers in the district and gave them an opportunity to buy additional grain from the west. At that time I was more interested in grain from the west. Many years we had over 100 carloads of grain from the west including wheat, oats, barley and mixed feeds. That fine plant is going down because Britain offered us starvation prices. I do not know if the minister could help us. Britain got flax from Latvia which offered it at dumping prices. We will not be able to carry on and we will have to close the plant. If that happens, a manufacturer from Canada or from any other democratic country in the world will be welcome to step in and start any kind of manufacturing plant there. We will rent or sell it at a sacrifice, perhaps 25 per cent of what it would normally cost. The plant would cost about $300,000 if one were to build it today.
Because I deal with at least 600 farmers a year and approximately 600 customers engaged in other occupations including labourers and business people within a radius of 60 miles of my home, I feel that I am qualified to speak about the needs of the farmer and what we should do for him. Not only should we assist in educating them but we should also improve the prices they receive for their goods. Many of the needed

Supply-Agriculture
improvements cost much money and the farmer requires sufficient money to carry on his operations.
I will complete my remarks in English in order to provide an opportunity for Englishspeaking hon. members to listen to me and try to understand. It will be easier for them than if I were to speak in French. I am interested in seeing the simultaneous translation system installed in the house because then it will be easier for me to speak in French. I want the English-speaking hon. members to know that I had to work 13 hours a day at the rate of 50 cents a day in order to go to school to learn the English language. I therefore feel I have done my duty and I must express the wish that more Englishspeaking people would make an effort to learn our language. We should not really have a translation system in the house. It is not natural. It is far more natural and interesting to listen to a person speak in his own language.
The Minister of Agriculture referred a moment ago to the fact that we import mutton and that the raising of sheep should be encouraged. Something should be done to raise the price of meat and wool. In my part of the country dogs are a serious menace to sheep. The destruction of flocks in my riding has been due mostly to dogs but in other districts sheep are menaced by bears and other animals. In some districts the farmers are compensated for sheep destroyed in this way but the price is very low.
I have explained my position. I am not a farmer but I still have 200 acres of farm land. I am a businessman. In my business I carry every important piece of goods from puzzles to bulldozers. Therefore, if any of my good friends need something for themselves or for their good wives they will be welcome at my home and they will be just as well served if they are Conservatives as if they were Grits.
If the minister wants to do something to help the farmers of this country I will give him a five-point program. First, the farm loan board should be permitted to lend money on a farm at 90 per cent of the appraised valuation, up to $10,000, and any amount over this at something around 70 per cent of the appraiser's evaluation. As it is now, the appraisers value the farms at only about 80 per cent of their value and allow very little on the buildings. Usually in the east and in the maritimes where we find mostly mixed farming, the buildings on the farms are much more expensive than the land. The interest should be reduced to 4 per cent on a 30-year payment and should be paid by the farmers in any amount at any time without notice. That is the practice [Mr. Gour.l
I carry out in my own business. They are always welcome to come after 12 o'clock noon and if it is not after seven o'clock in the morning we call it the day before. Therefore, I make the suggestion that the farmer be given the chance to pay without notice at any time before the due day. This encourages them to pay and it would be an advantage for them to do so.
My second suggestion would be to ask the Minister of Agriculture to use his influence on the Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Trade and Commerce so that they may be more careful in the words they use when they talk about diversion of trade from our friends and neighbours, the United States of America. Diversification does not bring anything to anybody. If they get dissatisfied on this question of diversion they may stop buying our cattle, our pork, our sheep, and so forth. At the present time the United States are buying our cattle and other animals, and that is the reason for our high prices. If tomorrow the United States were to stop buying our cattle the price of cattle would drop by 50 per cent. I defy anybody to say anything else because I have had the experience of dealing with farmers for 35 years. There has been too much talk about diverting trade from our good neighbours. I would prefer that we did not talk so much about it because our friends may get dissatisfied. Good business people do not talk along that line.
My third suggestion, Mr. Chairman, is that there should be an increase in freight subsidies of $3 a ton on all feed and grain from the west which are shipped to the maritime provinces and to Ontario and Quebec so that the farmers may be encouraged to feed more of the grain. Unfortunately, the people of my riding are selling their cattle unfinished. Some of those cattle are only a year or two years old. The farmers do not make a profit when they sell their cattle that young. We should buy western grain and feed it to our cattle and sell those cattle to our friends to the south and to our people at home. In that way our people would use more western grain and would thereby help the farmers of the west and at the same time make more money for themselves. This would encourage our farmers to give better grazing to their cattle and raise more of them. This applies also to the raising of chickens and pigs. Too many farmers are selling their cattle too young and in an unfinished state to the United States and by doing this they lose their profits.
My fourth suggestion is that we should have a farm credit bank system which should be extended to the fishermen and potato growers

as well as to the small business operators. With the farm loan legislation and the farm development legislation we are in need of a farm credit banking system under which the government will guarantee short term loans of the bank at around 90 per cent and permit the farmers to obtain loans when they are in urgent need, at a low rate of interest. Such legislation should permit the government to send government experts to supervise the farms and advise the farmers. This is one of the great needs of the farmer. They should be in a position to receive help from people who can advise them. That advice could be given in conjunction with advice from the agricultural representatives of the Ontario government.
My fifth suggestion is that the so-called stabilization farm price should be raised on cheese, beef, pork, eggs, poultry, butter and skim milk at least 10 per cent higher than it is now, because the stabilization price is no good to the farmers at the moment because it is less than the price at which they have been selling their farm products for the past two years. In the meantime the cost of operating the farms has gone up from 15 per cent to 25 per cent and this applies also to the things which the farmer has to buy. A cheese factory in my riding is not selling cheese at all at the moment. They have not sold any cheese for two months; they are stuck with it. The price of machinery and the price of everything else has gone up. I keep everything in my store and I am in a position to know what I am talking about. I have a report from my manager which indicates that the cost of shoes, pants, and everything else has gone up. I will not name all of the commodities. The cost of labour has also gone up. Nobody wants to work on a farm any more. They work in the city. It is easy work in most cases and they work only 40 hours a week. The farmers, unfortunately, have to work on Sunday and holidays, on confederation day, Canada day, not Dominion day. The farmer has to work on those days as well, and there is no holiday for him. The prices of everything the farmer has to buy have risen.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I submit this idea to the minister in the hope that he and the government will give it every consideration. They will do so if they wish to do something to help the farmers remain on the farms and keep their sons with them. We have to be careful to encourage them to produce on a high scale. It is estimated that the population of Canada will greatly increase in the next few years. We hope to be in a position to supply food for our own people as well as the people in other parts of the world, and in that way keep

communism away from us. In this way we shall be able to prove to other nations, as we have in the past, that we in Canada are doing our duty in every way. We will show that we want to be friendly with every country which wants to give liberty and freedom to its subjects.
I know that my friend, the Minister of Agriculture, will take these remarks as a friend's opinion. I am not playing politics in connection with this question. I am only hoping that the farmer will receive more.
I know when I say that that my city electors will say, "Gour is for the farmer." I do say that the more prosperous the farmers of this country are, the more prosperous the country will be. Then, too, if the farmer is prosperous he will not go into the city and take jobs which the people in the city need. Therefore everything within reason should be done for the farmer because that will be of advantage to every citizen in this country; that is my opinion, and I think I am right. It is because I think I am right that I am saying these things to the minister.
I ask the minister to try to convince the rest of the cabinet of these facts, as I am sure he is convinced of them. The time for politics is over. It may be too bad, but you are elected for the next four years, so there is time to do something.

Since I come from a province whose economy is, to a very large extent, dependent on agriculture, I should like to refer in this opening discussion to several phases of that economy which are vital to us at this time. One of our biggest problems is that of obtaining adequate farm credit facilities, and in that respect I include funds necessary for rehabilitation. In speaking on agriculture at the last session I outlined the alarming decrease in the number of farms being operated in our province. As we all know, this results in a serious decline in the general economy of any province, a great loss in production, and eventually a great expense in returning those farms to a state of production which we feel will be necessary at a later period. One of the chief reasons for such an exodus from the farms is the lack of proper credit facilities.
The provisions of the Canadian Farm Loan Act have long been outdated and fail to serve the needs of many of our farm population. I would suggest that it is extremely urgent that steps be taken to either bring this board up to date or replace it with a body which will meet the needs for farm credit under present day conditions. If we are to return these abandoned farms to production, it is necessary in most cases that we inaugurate

Supply-Agriculture
a scheme which will allow young farmers, or immigrants, to take over these farms under certain conditions and return them to a productive paying basis. For some years now, many of us have followed closely the successful operation of the Veterans Land Act, as administered by the Department of Veterans Affairs. We feel strongly that if arrangements were made to set up good prospective farmers, under conditions such as those provided under the Veterans Land Act, well supervised and controlled, then we would have a rehabilitation scheme which would be eminently successful. I hope steps will be taken soon along these lines which will achieve, in a large measure, the desire that many of us have for the repopulation of these abandoned farms.
Closely allied to such a program should be the experience and information derived from investigations into land use. I know there has been a committee of the other place studying this problem, and I hope that there will soon be tangible results from their investigations. Here again, I would urge the government to pursue their policy of investigation into this matter, as it would be extremely helpful to any rehabilitation scheme.
One of the major crops in our province is potatoes. Having been very familiar with this phase of our agricultural industry as a dealer and a small grower since world war II, I feel I should make some comment concerning present conditions in that industry within our province. First of all, I must say from practical experience that the humble potato is probably one of the most difficult products in the world to market. The potato market is a most sensitive one for a large variety of reasons which would take a long time to explain. Most of our farmers agree that potatoes are a highly speculative product in which to deal, and appreciate that if a permanent support price is placed under the product that policy could be fraught with many dangers. Of course, our farmers would expect to be subjected to many controls. In general, they do not wish to be placed in this position. However, they do expect that when an emergency arises it will be treated with due consideration.
During the past year we have had an abnormally large crop, not so much as a result of any increase in acreage as the result of ideal growing conditions throughout the whole season. The average price has been fairly good, and in midwinter was reasonably high. Unfortunately, because of our insular position and the fact that we are serviced by only one railway, as well as the fact that reefer cars have only one-way freight, we are seldom, if ever, in a surplus position with regard to this type of rolling stock. During [Mr. Macdonald (Kings) .1
the past winter, when prices were high, our farmers shipped to the capacity of reefer cars available. When the price started to drop they still kept shipping at a high rate. Unfortunately, as a result of the mildness of the winter, there was an abnormally early closing of the side roads and paved highways to heavy traffic. Many of our farmers were unable to ship until a much later date because of the load restrictions on highways, the early calling in of snowplows, and the unusually muddy conditions of the roads for a long period. This left many of our farmers, who normally do not ship until midwinter or later, in the awkward position of not being able to dispose of their potatoes.
I have mentioned earlier the extreme sensitivity of the potato market which is due to many factors pertaining to the marketing of potatoes throughout the whole of the North American continent. In some years we have new and entirely different factors entering the picture. This year one which seemed to have a great deal of influence was the manipulation of the New York mercantile exchange. At any rate, prices had a continual downward trend from mid-winter, with a dull and sluggish market which would not absorb the potatoes being offered.
As a result a number of our farmers were caught with fairly large holdings on their farms. The potato marketing board in our province then asked for some assistance to market the balance of the crop. After several submissions a figure of 45 cents per 75 pounds bulk on the farm was offered. Keeping in mind that this was a distress measure, as a number of farmers had been fortunate enough to market all or most of their crop at reasonably good prices, the price offered by the stabilization board was fairly adequate. Yet, in view of the fact that some farmers were in the unfortunate position of being located where they could not have shipped, it was felt by many, including my colleagues from Prince Edward Island and myself, that the price should have been somewhat higher.
In fairness it might be noted, however, that it does compare more favourably than that offered at the beginning of the marketing season of 1955, when the prices offered were first 15 cents, 20 cents and 25 cents per bushel and later 20 cents, 25 cents and 30 cents per bushel over a marketing period of three phases. It must be remembered that this price was for the whole of the crop in that year, whereas we were asking for a distress price to look after the tail end of our potato crop. In view of the small amount of money spent in assisting the potato grower as compared to the amount used in

supporting other phases of the industry, we did not feel averse to requesting support- and fairly generous support-in an instance such as this. The price support to be granted has been settled for this season, and I do hope that, if the occasion again arises when support is needed, we shall be dealt with in a generous manner by the government and its official advisers.
Our agricultural picture is very closely interwoven with our transport problems. Although we have a great advantage with regard to isolation from diseases among our farm crops and cattle, we are at a distinct disadvantage where importation of feeds is concerned and, of course, in the carrying of our goods to market.
As I have on the order paper a resolution on the Northumberland causeway which I hope will come up for discussion, I will not deal with that phase of our transportation problem at the present time. However, for reasons I have just mentioned, I should like to deal briefly with present services; particularly that provided by the existing railroads and ferries.
As in many other parts of Canada, our rail service has been curtailed, with the approval of the board of transport commissioners, and I feel that it has been cut down too much, to a point where it is to the disadvantage financially of both the railways and our people, particularly our farm people. This is especially so in the constituency of Kings which I have the honour to represent. During the winter I made a trip on each of the three main lines in our county, familiarizing myself with the service from the viewpoint of the train crews, station agents and the travelling public. It is strongly urged that the present daily winter service be set up one month earlier in the fall and run one month later in the spring. In that way it would be providing many places with a service which would allow shippers of produce and other bulk products to compete on the same footing with those in other sections of the province, and it would not cost the railways any more than does the present irregular shortened service of the summer months.
Our passenger and vehicle service at both ferries has continued to grow regularly each season, and the present service at both Borden and Wood island is inadequate. A new boat has been provided for Wood island which will assist in that service greatly and by this fall, on the completion of the causeway survey, we should perhaps be in a better position to decide whether or not a new one will be necessary also at Borden. When the causeway is built there will still be great pressure for greater outlets in the eastern
Supply-Agriculture
part of the province. I would suggest that strong consideration be given then to the transfer of some of the facilities now at Borden to the port of Georgetown. This port is the finest one in the province with almost year round ice free conditions. A connecting link from here to Pictou in Nova Scotia would be a practical proposition and would provide an all year round and very much needed service to the eastern sections of Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia. It would provide this section of our province with better and more accessible markets for farm products, as well as a better service for our tourists and the travelling public generally.
It would be greatly appreciated, Mr. Chairman, if the government would give every consideration to these major farm problems which I have dealt with briefly. They are chiefly the rehabilitation of our abandoned farms, with due consideration of the Veterans Land Act as a model a wider expansion of farm credit facilities; progress in land use study; due consideration to adequate prices for support when warranted; and any assistance which could be provided in drawing attention to the importance to our transportation problems.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I have been very much
surprised this afternoon to note the usage the minister makes of certain words. He refers always to a moderate decrease and yet when he speaks of the same sum of money, if it is an increase, it is a substantial increase. I think that probably explains fairly well what the policy of the government in the past year has been with regard to agriculture. Where there is an increase, it is substantial but where there is a decrease of the same amount, it is very moderate. I think the farmers will eventually be wondering just where the substantial increase arises.
Some of the members have asked why I should be speaking on agriculture. There are a great number of new Conservative members from agricultural fields who probably do not know that in northern Ontario we have what is called the little clay belt which is probably one of most outstanding and most fertile agricultural areas in all of Canada. Western members may be interested to learn that this area which is in northern Ontario and-that there is a great quantity of available agricultural land-suitable for mixed farming. We have many farmers who farmed in the west. It may be of interest to hon. members to learn that when our house leader came to northern Ontario last week he met two or three farmers near whom he had farmed in his

Supp ly-A griculture
own area but who are now farming in northern Ontario. It is a mixed farming
area. Unless this particular government does something about the problems of wheat I am quite sure they will be able to explain to some of the new members who wish to go into farming that they will be able to go into northern Ontario, if the price of wheat continues to fall.
This government since its inception has continually tried to maintain, in my opinion, the poor conditions under which the farmers have existed for the last five or six years and they have striven very hard to do that. I am surprised to hear that some consideration has been given to agriculture when we note the amount provided in the estimates that are now being discussed. In the 195758 estimates under a Liberal government $87 million was the amount involved in the agriculture estimates, and in the current ones, those for 1958-59, only $90 million is involved. So that if this government has done such a great deal for agriculture and for the people in that field, they have done it or hope to do it with the sum of $3 million over and above the former estimates.
The minister made a good deal of the Agricultural Stabilization Act and he mentioned some of the things which had been happening. On page 2075 of Hansard for July 9 last he had this to say:
As I have said, I think a great deal of the improvement has been as the result of policies followed by this government, including the introduction of the Agricultural Stabilization Act.
He goes on to say something about a formula and the general opinion has been expressed during and since the last election that this Agricultural Stabilization Act did have a formula. I think it is very interesting to note the words of the minister when he referred to this formula and when he was comparing the changes in the new act with the provisions of the old act. He said:
A formula was included for establishing a base price for any agricultural commodities.
He does not say the base price for these agricultural commodities was established on a formula but he says that the formula was included for the establishment of this base price. I suggest there is a great deal of difference between a formula used in establishing a base price and a formula for the establishment of that base price. I presume that when you have a stabilized price you do have a formula but I do not think there is any formula which has any relationship to anything else in this base price.
The minister goes on to mention an advisory board comprised of representatives from farm organizations and outlines the general intentions of the act and so on, but I would

like to know from the minister before his estimates are completed how often this stabilization board is meeting, what they are doing and just what they have accomplished which was not accomplished by the previous act.
I know that the officials of the government, in particular of the department concerned, who have been appointed to administer the act were the people who administered the old act and I have personally found them very courteous and helpful at all times. Let us look at some of the prices which have been stabilized, however. It is generally understood that prices were to be stabilized at 80 per cent of the average price for the last ten years and it has been pointed out that butter, for instance, has been stabilized at 107 per cent, steers and lambs at 80 per cent and the highest percentage quoted was 112 per cent. We also know that in the case of many of these commodities the floor price established is considerably higher than formerly under this formula- as the minister calls it-of 80 per cent. Some commodities, however, were receiving greater prices prior to the introduction of this act and it is probable that prices received do not have too much relationship to this legislation.
We believe that the Conservative government has done very little to stabilize agriculture in our country. In my own particular area, and I think this applies across Canada, the number of people leaving the farms has not decreased since this government came to power. In fact, their problems are just as great today as they were under the old administration; the standard of living in rural areas has not improved and neither have conditions generally.
As in all other parts of our economy the prices of consumer goods have continued to rise, which has forced up the cost of living and these prices are continuing to rise. Yet we are given an assurance that conditions are improving. I believe and my party believes that the solution to some of these problems is the implementation of a parity price. In the last few years there has been an increased interest in deficiency payments but it would appear to me that deficiency payments are merely a substitute for a parity price, the only difference being that a deficiency payment is paid on a product already sold-

Would the hon. member permit a question? Would he mind giving the house his definition of parity of prices, that is to say the C.C.F.'s definition? I have been wondering about that and I would like

to hear it from the hon. member this afternoon because some of us may be answering him in this debate today.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I would be more than pleased to do so, but I would first like to say that there have been many explanations of parity prices because all political parties, unfortunately, have used this term in the course of every election with which I have been concerned.
I believe and my party believes that a parity price is a price which will take care of cost of production on a regional basis. It would mean, for example, with respect to a dairy product such as whole milk, where it is not called a parity price but that is what it means, that you would have to take into consideration the wholesale index, the weekly wage index, the commodities and services used by farmers index, the price of butter fat index, the prices of condensed products index and the prices of cheese index. You would have to add up all these figures and put the total over 100 in order to arrive at a base. We feel that account must be taken of all facets of cost of production, including farm labour, cost of living, cost of machinery, a certain return on investment and allowance for interest on loans and all those things which are necessary in order to produce your product. Your selling price must be equal to this amount and we do not consider that profits should enter into this question. A parity price would only be cost of production which would include all the divisions I have outlined.

May I ask a supplementary question of the hon. gentleman? I am sure he knows that the cost of producing a bushel of wheat in some sections is less than others, and would he take into account the regional costs?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Yes, it would be on a regional basis.
Would the hon. gentleman say the cost of producing a bushel of wheat even in the same community might vary from farm to farm?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I would say it would.
Mr. Chairman, on a point of order, I am wondering if this edifying debate is in order on the minister's estimates.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
The Canadian Federation of Agriculture carry out surveys and they at one time had the services of an exceptionally fine economist who, unfortunately, has passed on. However, they have the benefit of considerable research and I am sure they could tell the hon. gentleman what he wishes to
Supply-Agriculture
know. These facts are all available and they could tell him exactly the average price of producing a bushel of wheat in any given area of the prairie provinces, or Ontario or the maritimes, for that matter. These are things which can be worked out and have in fact been worked out and if the hon. member represents a wheat growing community I am sure he would be most interested to know what is the formula price for wheat in his particular area.
We believe that no farmer, and for that matter no person, should be asked to produce a product for nothing or in respect of which over a given period of time he is in effect losing money. Those in labour a few years ago implemented a very similar program to this when they attached to their wages the matter of the cost of living. They computed the cost of living on the dominion bureau of statistics figures, and every time the cost of living went up a point they had their wages increased. We feel that if the farmer is going to maintain his position on the farm -if that is the wish of the Conservative government-they are going to have to do something not only to see that the farmer gets along as well as he did last year, because that was not very good in my area, but that he gets a much better deal than he has had in the last two or three years and that he returns to the plane he was existing on in the years between 1945 and 1951 when he came closer to maintaining a parity price than ever before. I do not think many farmers throughout Canada would say that that parity price between 1945 and 1951 was a bad thing.
There are many other considerations which the minister must take into consideration. Certainly, for the benefit of those members from the west who have not been here before, I think they will be very concerned with this matter of crop insurance. I understand that in the west there is a serious drought condition. In my area it is not a drought condition. We have had lots of rain, but we have not had much good weather and we are faced with a poor hay crop, and unless conditions improve we are not going to have good grain either. Some consideration must be given to the stabilization of the products that agriculture is producing. The agricultural producers of this country want to market as good a product as possible. To enable them to do that and maintain a standard for Canadian products that will sell across the world the government is going to have to insist on much better grading and much better marketing than we have now. We have had over the last year a great deal of difficulty concerning bacon. That one commodity, bacon, has been done up in packages

Sup p ly-A griculture
and it looks very nice. The packages have had red cellophane on them, and you buy a package of bacon and think you are getting good bacon but you end up getting mostly lard. If we are going to work for international markets or to increase local markets we are going to have to provide the means whereby we can provide a much more stabilized product than now.
I am very pleased to hear from the agriculture committee that they are going to be discussing the matter of credit for agricultural loans. This is one of the great problems that we face in northern Ontario and I am sure we are facing it across the country, and while I do not want to discuss this matter at any length I do hope that the minister will give consideration to providing for the farmers loans on a similar basis to those which are provided for under the Veterans Land Act which have in most cases worked out very satisfactorily. It has been apparent to the Veterans Land Act authority that they must to some extent supervise the credit they are extending, and there comes a time when credit must be extended beyond what is considered now satisfactory under our chattel mortgages and loan mortgages, and I think the Veterans Land Act has found some solution to this question.
The matter of crop insurance is, I suggest, going to be very important to western farmers. It has been said that they have four or five years of wheat built up in their yards or in their granaries, but I am quite sure that they are depending this year on a crop that they may not produce. While this matter is provincial in scope and has been handled by some of the provinces, I think the federal government has an obligation to provide leadership for those provinces who have not seen fit to look after this matter on their own behalf. If we are sincere in our talk about extending benefits to farmers under other acts, I think we could provide unemployment insurance in a manner in which it could be provided to a farmer, namely by the implementation of crop insurance.
Again, we are concerned with the matter of the wheat surplus. Some people maintain that with a better price for agricultural products there might be a surplus. At the present time, and for a number of years, the only major surplus in agriculture in Canada has been in wheat, and according to reports that surplus may not be as much this year as it has been in other years. But this is, again, a matter which needs a great deal of consideration and sympathetic study. This is a commodity maintained by the federal government and the federal government must take care of that portion of the product that must be sold on the international markets. We are

pleased with the work that has been done in this field, but certainly would support any constructive decision that is made to have a two-price system on wheat, where one price could be available on a competitive basis on the international market and the other one handled perhaps under the Agricultural Prices Support Act where we think it should have been put in the first place.
Another problem which faces agriculture is this matter of farm efficiency. There have been a number of very comprehensive articles written about this. The Conservative candidate in my area was very concerned about where the farmer was going, whether he was efficient enough to operate and just how he could be helped, and one of the ways in which big business is helping the farmer is through this matter of vertical integration. While this has taken place and some of our farmers have accepted it because of cash restrictions and because they have to borrow money from the bank in order to develop, they have signed contracts with feed companies and other companies such as packing companies that are less than what would be called desirable. Unless some consideration is given to this matter the small farmer who has been the backbone of agriculture in Canada for years will gradually disappear and we will find the farmer in the position of a hired man for the local packing company or for the local feed dealer.
Some consideration must be given to examining this vertical integration program. Legislation should be developed that would be much more effective in dealing with combines which would take place and could take place very easily in the feed industry and in the packing industry where they are supplying the money. If the farmer is going to be forced into this vertical integration, then I think the federal government has an obligation to protect the farmer and enact legislation that will prohibit the abuses present in the contracts farmers are now signing, and make it imperative that if a farmer is going to sign this type of contract he will be at least protected so that at the end of the year he will have a decent standard of living.
On this same business there is a conclusion that has been reached that I think will be of interest. It is from an organization that I do not usually quote. It is the Searle Grain Company Limited. I am quoting from a booklet entitled "This matter of farm efficiency -a commentary":
It has been said that farming can no longer be considered a way of life, that it is strictly a business which must be run on strictly businesslike lines. We venture to say, however, that desirable and necessary as it will always be to aim for the greatest efficiency possible, farming will still remain very much a way of life to many.

Life is made up, after all, of apparent inconsistencies and that is why the human desire to cling to farming in the face of difficulties is something which cannot be explained in terms of the dollars and cents return any more than it can be fully understood by those who concern themselves with efficiency. The present trend toward larger farming operations will undoubtedly proceed but with two-thirds of our prairie farms still under three-quarters of a section in size there is little doubt that for many years to come the moderate sized or relatively small holdings will continue to occupy an important place in the whole farming industry in western Canada. To our way of thinking this is very desirable.
I suggest this is desirable to the agricultural industry of all Canada. We endorse it and urge the minister to take some steps to see that it comes about.
A problem has developed in my area which I should like to bring to the attention of the minister. We have been farming in northern Ontario for approximately 50 years. The farmland has been heavily worked. The prices that have existed in years gone by with a very few exceptions have been such that the farmer has not been able to take steps to replace the minerals in the depleted soil. Such action is now necessary. Mixed farming takes more from the soil than does the type of farming that is done in the west. Now the farmer is faced with increased costs for providing commercial fertilizer and agricultural limestone.
There is a federal statute in existence called the Agricultural Limestone Subvention Act, revised April 1, 1951. This is a joint program involving the railway companies, the provincial governments and the federal government. Its purpose is to provide at the lowest possible cost agricultural limestone for use by farmers subsidized with respect to freight rates. The railways have made a reduction for the farmer who imports agricultural limestone. The reduction is 25 per cent. The Ontario government in southern Ontario pays 75 per cent of the reduced freight rate up to a maximum of $2.50 per ton. In northern Ontario the provincial government will pay 75 per cent of the reduced freight rate with no limit and the purchaser will pay the balance. The federal government will pay 60 per cent of the provincial contribution to the freight rate for the hauling of agricultural limestone when billed by the provincial government. If the limestone is hauled by truck from the source to the farmer the federal will pay five cents per ton up to a maximum of $2 which would be 40 ton miles. This has been advantageous to the people of northern Ontario. They have had to use increasing quantities of limestone which they have purchased by the carload through farm co-operatives, the federation of agriculture and the farmers' union. They have
Supp ly-A griculture
appreciated this arrangement. Because commercial fertilizer falls in the same category as agricultural limestone and because they have to buy fertilizer in such large quantities the farmers in that area would like the act extended to apply to fertilizer as well. This would mean that the farmers could put more fertilizer on the land.
From my experience with farmers I know they are the original conservationists. The farmer owns his land. He likes farm life and puts all the money he can into his farm. If the coverage of the agricultural limestone subvention policy were to be extended the farmers themselves would make an increased contribution to the betterment of the country and would increase the production of agricultural products on their farms.
May I conclude by expressing the hope that in the near future the Minister of Agriculture will introduce legislation that is not a copy of the kind of legislation the Liberal government implemented many years ago. Farm prices have been steadily decreasing. Farmers are leaving their farms in great numbers. The agricultural economy of Canada in my opinion is one of our greatest heritages. It is a renewable resource of which we should be proud. We should take good care of it and give the industry all the assistance we can.

Mr. Chairman, a week or so ago when I addressed myself to the coal problems of the maritime provinces it was pointed out by the minister concerned that I was an ex-inspector of fisheries attempting to speak on the coal problems of the mari-times. If this afternoon I participate briefly in this debate on the first item of the estimates of the Department of Agriculture I hope I will not be accorded similar treatment by the Minister of Agriculture.
When introducing the first item of his estimates on Wednesday the minister made a general statement on the situation of agriculture particularly during the past year. In his statement, the minister stated that farm cash income had declined slightly from 1956 level but it was $47 million higher than the average for the ten-year period 19481957, and higher than the amount realized in five years out of this ten-year period. In order to make his statement clear and logical, the minister should also have mentioned the increase in population which took place during that same period and which normally would mean a much larger consumption of our agricultural products.
With an actual farming population of approximately 17 per cent of the total population of this country, it is true that the productivity per man hour has advanced far

Supply-Agriculture
more rapidly in agriculture than in any other industry in Canada. It is a well-known fact that our country today is almost self-sufficient in the production of food for its growing population, with food imports averaging only approximately 4 per cent of our total farm production. It is therefore logical that an industry which affects such a large percentage of our population, with total gross revenue of approximately $2J billion per year, should receive considerable attention from the parliament of Canada. The total estimates for the present fiscal year for the Department of Agriculture amount to approximately $97 million, or less than 2 per cent of the total budget for the present fiscal year.
In the course of his statement, the minister stated that a considerable number of commodities had been stabilized under the Agricultural Stabilization Act and had so far authorized 16 products in addition to turkeys and potatoes which were authorized under the Agricultural Prices Support Act. This report shows that out of the 16 commodities quoted, 11 have been supported at a percentage below the 100 per cent average base price for the last ten years, and in fact, five of these commodities have been supported at the minimum price of 80 per cent based on prices paid for the last ten years.
Before this first item is passed by this committee could the minister inform us what was the total amount paid under the agricultural prices stabilization program from January of this year to June 30? We will also be interested to know how much was paid in subsidy, or deficiency payments for asparagus and soybeans.
Now, Mr. Chairman, while the number of cattle exported in 1957, as stated by the minister, was seven times as high as the exports for the previous year, we must also take into consideration the fact that on account of this large increase in exports the Canadian consumer is paying from 25 per cent to 30 per cent more for beef than he was paying a year ago. This is adding, accordingly, to the cost of living and we must also take into consideration the fact that this increase in export of cattle is only a temporary one and could easily be reversed when the United States have increased their production, as they are doing now.
Notwithstanding the accusations made by members of the present government about the legislation brought in by the previous administration, we must all admit that the present policy of the government is based almost entirely on the sound foundation of Liberal legislation. The only major changes made since June, 1957, are the cash advances on farm-stored grain and amendments to the Agricultural Stabilization Act.

Measures such as the freight assistance policy, the Farm Improvement Loans Act, the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, the Maritime Marshland Rehabilitation Act were all enacted by the previous administration. The Liberal administration also assisted and supported the Canadian wheat board through vigorous sales policies, with wheat sales in previous years reaching record proportions.
As I have just stated, it is evident that the present government so far has done nothing more than build on the sound legislation introduced by the previous administration. We of the official opposition realize that the ever-increasing farm production in Canada requires a new approach to the problem of agriculture, with proposals that will be of long range benefit to our farmers and which will assure them the place which they deserve in our economy and in our national life.
The importance of a national policy on farm problems, farm credit and others, must be one of the main concerns of the present government. It is the duty of the government of this country to maintain a healthy and efficient agriculture and this cannot be done unless prices paid for farm commodities can assure our farmers a fair profit for their farming operations. With our increase in population our agriculture . should become more and more stabilized but for the time being our farmers want constructive action from the present government.
While certain farm commodities have been included for price support or deficiency payments under the agricultural stabilization bill, other important commodities have been left out from the permanent list and may be included only after acceptance by the governor in council. It may be all right to support such commodities as asparagus or soybeans, but we from the maritime provinces want to know why potatoes are not included on the permanent list of commodities coming under this act or at least why our potato growers are not given the protection received by growers of other products in other sections of the country.
They have had a great deal of protection; a lot of money has been paid out to them.

The minister seems to be satisfied with the protection which has been given so far. Unfortunately, our farmers are not of the same opinion. The Prime Minister has said on numerous occasions that "there is a distress price in Canada below which all agricultural prices cannot fall." The potato is an important commodity for farmers in Prince Edward Island and New

Brunswick and our farmers have a right to expect the same protection which is being given to farm producers in other sections of the country. The recent offer made to Prince Edward Island farmers, averaging 33 cents a bushel for their potatoes, is not sufficient. It is not a sufficient offer to our producers and the government without delay should come out with a farm policy for our potato growers.
Another commodity which has been given the run around by the Minister of Agriculture is the pulpwood sold on the small farms in eastern Canada. We all realize that a large number of our small farm owners depend on the sale of pulpwood cut from their woodlots as a source of ready cash or revenue to meet the payment of their municipal taxes and other urgent obligations. Those small farmers are receiving today for their pulpwood a price which is far from satisfactory and which barely meets their expenses of cutting this pulpwood and taking it to the roadside.
On January 21 last, as reported at page 3809 of Hansard, for the 1957-58 session, during the course of the debate on the agricultural products prices stabilization bill I asked the minister the following question:
I would appreciate it if the minister would be more specific and explain why he is opposed to the inclusion of pulpwood as one of the commodities to be covered by the bill, or can he assure us that pulpwood could be included under subparagraph (ii) of clause 2, "any other natural or processed product of agriculture designated by the governor in council."
On that occasion I received the following reply from the minister:
Yes, Mr. Chairman, Clause 2 provides for support prices being established for any agricultural commodity which is accepted by the governor in council on the advice of the committee and of the board as one which should be supported.
This, Mr. Chairman, could be considered as a rather vague reply, but during the political campaign, while speaking in Rimouski on February 27, the Prime Minister said, as reported in the Toronto Daily Star of February 27, 1958, something which was rather more specific, and I quote:
I hope that the advisory committee and the stabilization board would give consideration to including farm-produced wood so that they will know the lowest price they will receive in a year in advance.
It is five o'clock, Mr. Chairman.
