subtopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY

speakeroldname: Mr. E. J. Broome (Vancouver South) moved
subtopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. S-6, respecting the Trans Mountain Oil Pipe Line Company.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill, as set out in the bill, is to subdivide each of the shares without nominal or par value into five shares without nominal or par value. Such a subdivision would result in a reduction in the unit price per share and a corresponding increase in the number of shares held by each shareholder and in the number of shares available for future issue. It is believed that the lower unit price and larger number of shares should encourage a wider distribution of the company's shares among investors in Canada and would facilitate future financing by the company. After this bill has passed second reading, I undertake that the officials of the company will be available to the members of the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines to explain the bill in detail.
Before I go on to the financing of the company, I should like to go into a certain amount of detail concerning the operation of Trans Mountain Oil Pipe Line Company and pipe line companies generally, so that the members of this house will have a knowledge of the oil pipe line industry. As hon. members will recall, Trans Mountain was incorporated by an act of parliament in 1951 for the purpose of transporting oil from Alberta to the Pacific coast. It was originally conceived and built as an all-Canadian line at a time when it was considered politically desirable that the oil reserves of Canada should be reserved for Canadian use. For this reason the terminus of the line was to be in the Vancouver area, with a provision for shipping any surplus oil to export markets by tanker or by barge. However, the fantastic growth in Canadian oil reserves soon made it apparent that development of these Canadian oil fields would be held back unless export markets were secured, and to this end Trans Mountain incorporated a wholly owned United States subsidiary, Trans Mountain Oil Pipe Line Corporation, which owns and operates the company's pipe line system in the state of Washington. This Washington system is connected to the refinery of the General Petroleum Corporation at Ferndale, and to the refinery at Anacortes of the Shell Oil Company, as well as to the new Texaco refinery which is presently being built in the same area. The total for these two refineries, excluding Texaco, will be 90,000 barrels a day.
When Trans Mountain was built approximately 2,500 men were engaged on the original construction of the project, of whom

90 per cent were Canadians who gained experience in the complexities of pipe line construction. Since the completion of the original line a number of substantial contracts have been awarded to Canadian construction companies, giving additional employment. In this regard, it might be well for members of the house to understand the purchasing policy of Trans Mountain Oil Pipe Line Company, which is set out in the purchasing manual as follows:
General policy is to purchase materials and equipment made in the following areas with preference given in the order they are shown:
1.	Canada-western area
2.	Canada-eastern area
3.	United Kingdom
4.	United States
5.	Other countries
The preference referred to is given only on the basis that materials and equipment are of equal quality and price.
Policy as regards distributors and wholesale houses will be to place orders for use in Alberta with firms located in the Edmonton area, wherever possible, and for British Columbia requirements with Vancouver firms. Consideration is also to be given Kamloops firms where they are able to compete.
In a most recent expansion of the system, two leading Canadian manufacturers of electrical equipment were given the opportunity of producing in Canada, for the first time, large capacity explosion-proof electric motors and complicated control systems for pipe line pump stations. When it is not possible to obtain our requirements from Canadian manufacturers the manual states preference is given to the United Kingdom and commonwealth suppliers. Every effort has been made and will be made to allow them to participate in our business. In some cases we have been able to delay our delivery dates in order that they might participate in this business.
As to the staff of the company, as called for in the Companies Act the majority of the directors are Canadians. In regard to the employment of other personnel for Trans Mountain, the employment policy from its very start has been to obtain qualified Canadian and British commonwealth personnel, with preference given to those with oil industry experience and especially pipe line experience. To this end, more than 2,000 applicants were reviewed during the hiring of the first 150 employees. Of these 150 Canadians and British commonwealth citizens very few had previous important pipe line experience. The company paid for and sent these men around to various pipe line companies, both in Canada and the United States, in order to gain this experience. At the present time Trans Mountain Pipe Line Company is wholly staffed with Canadian personnel. This should
Private Bills
be a bit of an object lesson to a lot of other pipe line companies who have not shown that same initiative.
Because of the publicity which has been given to pipe lines and pipe line matters, Mr. Speaker, both in the press and in parliament over the past few years, it would seem desirable at this time to say a few words about an oil pipe line as compared to a gas pipe line. On land, the main arteries of transportation of both petroleum and natural gas are the pipe lines. At this moment, I am reading from the submission of Trans Mountain Oil Pipe Line Company to the Borden commission. These pipe lines are similar in size, extent and general trunkline constitution. It would appear that, generally speaking, the public does not differentiate between the two. However, there are characteristic differences which are of major importance when considering government regulation and control as well as such matters as finance and operation.
Oil pipe lines generally transport a commodity that is owned by others, a raw material that is eventually delivered to a refinery for further processing into many products before reaching the consumer. Gas pipe lines, on the other hand, frequently function as public utilities, owning the material they transport and delivering it as a finished product. An oil pipe line frequently has no guaranteed business and is essentially a high-risk venture; a gas pipe line, before construction gets under way, generally has long-term contracts for both supply and delivery that will guarantee the high load factor essential to economic operation, thus making it a relatively safe undertaking. In fact, in the case of Trans Mountain it was necessary, because of the risk element, to obtain from the major backers of the project deficiency agreements which will be further explained when I deal with the financing of this company.
In the United States, controversy over the pros and cons of ownership and control of pipe lines by the major integrated companies has existed since the early days of the oil industry. Out of this controversy have come such regulatory measures as the Elkins act, prohibiting rebates, the consent decree regarding permissible dividend payments and various Sherman act anti-trust cases. Divorcement of pipe lines and disintegration of major companies have been seriously considered by the authorities concerned. In this regard, I should like to refer to the Merrill foundation for the advancement of financial knowledge which financed the work of Mr. Leslie Cookenboo, who produced a study on this very important subject. This study is contained in this book entitled

Private Bills
"Crude Oil Pipe Lines and Competition in the Oil Industry". I should like to quote from page 143 where Mr. Cookenboo, in discussing public policy and public control of pipe lines, has this to say:
A similar development, which is even closer to the best that any public policy could hope to achieve, is illustrated by the two Canadian lines mentioned above-
Namely Trans Mountain Oil Pipe Line Company and Interprovincial.

which were built under special permits from the Canadian government.
He goes on further to state that in these lines the financing was shared by independents and majors alike as well as public participation. He closes his paragraph on page 143 by stating this:
If future crude lines built in the United States were to imitate those built in Canada (most of the ownership is by United States companies or their subsidiaries), then there would be little ground for complaint about major exclusion of the market-oriented independent refiners from crude supplies.
Again on page 168 he states:
-the latest such joint venture,-
That is of independents and majors combined.
-Trans Mountain is an almost ideal example of how a pipe line should be built-
I should now like to turn to the financial structure of the company. When Trans Mountain was first financed it was based on an estimated completion cost of approximately $80 million, and it was decided that $65 million should be produced by the sale of bonds and $15 million by the sale of shares. Shares to the number of 450,000 were sold to the public at $10 per share to yield to the company $9.50 per share after deduction of underwriters' fees. The remainder of the shares issued originally were sold directly at $10 per share. With respect to the 450,000 shares sold to the public, the underwriters were asked to effect a wide distribution to Canadian purchasers. That this objective was accomplished is evidenced by the fact that the first shareholders' list included over 5,000 names; and I believe that number has increased to date, to something in the neighbourhood of 7,000 names. The shares were not offered for sale in the United States and no registration of the shares of this company has been effected with the United States securities and exchange commission. I may say that this again is from the submission to the Borden commission.
The prospectus of the company contained a clear warning of the risk and speculative nature of the undertaking. Because of this an important added feature is the fact that all the bonds issued are guaranteed by deficiency

agreements entered into between the company and the six major oil company shareholders. Those shareholders are Imperial Oil Limited; Shell Oil Company of Canada, Limited; Canadian Gulf Oil Company; Standard Oil Company of British Columbia, Limited; Union Oil Company of California and Richfield Oil Corporation. These companies are referred to as deficiency agreement guarantors. In other words, these companies have to guarantee the bondholders. That is, if the pipe line did not make a profit, and if it did not carry its charges, then these companies would have to make good to the bond holders. In addition, a group of independents signed deficiency agreements but these agreements were subject to lapse on December 31, 1956.
The effect of that is rather interesting, Mr. Speaker, in that the shareholding as of March 27, 1958 as compared to December 31, 1951, varies as follows. On December 31, 1951 some 670,000 shares were held by the major oil companies which were guarantors under the deficiency agreement. That number has dropped by only 100,000 shares to 570,000 shares as of March 27, 1958. However, the group of independents and smaller oil companies-and I am referring to oil company shareholders-which at December 31, 1951 owned 250,000 shares now own only 53,025 shares. This means that those shares have now a wider distribution than they had at the time when the company was first formed.
The intent of the bill is to divide the shares five for one in order to give a broader base in the way of participation by Canadians in the holding of shares of this company. This participation is considered to be good policy on the part of the company. I have tried to stress the Canadian nature of the company, the Canadian nature of their operations and the way that they are operating for the good of this country, in the way that I think a Canadian company should operate.
This bill was before parliament in 1957. At that time it was suggested that the treasury had 3,500,000 shares approximately and that this wider distribution could be effected simply by issuing those shares to present shareholders. Mr. Speaker, that procedure would not effect wider distribution in the way that this amendment will effect it. As I have pointed out, the oil companies which are guarantors of the line hold 670,000 shares, or rather 570,000 shares as of today's date. That would simply mean that the treasury stock would be turned over in relation to the present shareholders and in fact it would be watering the stock. The company prefers to do it in this way which

in effect is simply taking a $50 bill and changing it into five ten-dollar bills so that it is easier to trade. There is no watering of the stock. There is simply the chance of wider distribution of the stock. The equity that was behind each share of stock will be behind it in the proportion of one to five for each new share of stock. In addition, the company will have in their treasury unissued shares which can be used as required in the way of gaining funds for future financing.
Mr. Speaker, there is in this bill nothing of a contentious nature. In the Vancouver area alone this company, through the facilities it provides, has developed a refining industry which at the present time has increased employment in British Columbia by about 750 persons engaged in the refinery and oil transportation business. The municipality of Burnaby has benefited to a marked degree by the building of this pipe line as has the economy of Canada, because this pipe line has provided an outlet for many millions of dollars' worth of oil to the northwestern states.
As I said before, the company is ready to go before the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines for the purpose of answering all questions and divulging all information which the committee may require. I would ask that hon. members pass this bill on second reading so that it may get into the committee stages.

Mr. Speaker, back on March 11 of last year, in rising to speak on a bill, as reported at page 2093 of Hansard of 1957, in my opening sentence I had this to say:
-I have listened with a great deal of interest to all the debate on this bill, because it has to do with a company that is connected with the oil business and because the exact effect of the bill now before us is to ask the authority of parliament to split shares.
I can commence my remarks this afternoon with exactly the same words because we are dealing with the same bill. It is obvious that the officials of Trans Mountain Oil Pipe Line Company are very keen on having this parliament give them authority to split their shares five to one. Their interest is shown not only by the fact that this bill was introduced in 1957, at which time it failed to pass this house, but that the company has seen fit to place it before parliament again at the present time. In addition to these facts we also recognize the interest of the officials between the non-passage of the bill in 1957 and its re-introduction at this present session because those officials have endeavoured to make their position understood, if I may put it that way, to those who successfully blocked the bill in 1957. I can say that because Mr. Morrison, the president, came
Private Bills
to see me in my office in Vancouver between sessions-in between elections, as a matter of fact-and also because the officials of the company asked to meet with our group in this House of Commons just a few days ago.
I am not making this statement in a critical way; I think it was most commendable of the officials to try to see that we have a full understanding of what they have in mind. I assure all members of this house that we not only listened with a great deal of interest to the information we were given but we asked a great many questions of the officials of the company. But we are still in some doubt as to just what is behind the proposal to split the shares five to one. This is a further reason why we have listened very carefully to the remarks of the hon. member who sponsored this bill.
I am certain that all hon. members noted the emphasis placed upon what I presume is the main intent behind the measure which is, in the words of the sponsor, a wider distribution of shares and, later on, he said that the splitting of five to one would give a broader base of share holdings. I am sure that is a commendable motive but, quite honestly, we in this group cannot tie in that motive with the declared policies of the officials of the company. A large portion of the outstanding shares are held by oil companies-I think the figure is 33 or 35 per cent-and I believe those companies are nine in number. We have been told by Trans Mountain Oil Pipe Line Company officials within the last few days that there is no intention on the part of the oil companies to dispose of their shares and therefore there can be no greater distribution or broader base, because if they intend to hang on to their shares-
May I explain that point?
If the hon. member wishes to say that I am giving wrong information, most certainly, but I do not think he does.
No.
So there is no broader base of distribution except that the oil companies will hold five times the number of shares they now have in their possession.
On the same equity.

I said they had no intention of selling but that their holdings would amount to just five times the number of shares with the same equity, that is right. There is therefore no broader base for distribution and that is my first point. Secondly, the officials told us right in this building just a few days ago that there was no intention in the foreseeable future of the issuance of further stock. That was not contemplated

Private Bills
If the companies are going to hold their shares and Trans Canada Oil Pipe Line Company is not going to issue any more shares, then on what basis is the passage of this bill going to give a greater distribution of shares or establish a broader base of shareholding? The position explained to us by the officials- and this was confirmed by the sponsor-is that the intent of splitting the shares is merely for the purpose I have just outlined so far as the foreseeable future is concerned.
We have been given to understand, and this was mentioned in brief by the sponsor of the bill, that in the event of the necessity of the expanding of the operations of this company it would be in a better position in connection with the issuance of shares in order to obtain additional capital if it could present to the buying public shares of smaller denomination than those presently existing. In other words, to use the same terminology as the sponsor of the bill, by changing a $50 bill to five $10 bills then on a stock-selling basis they might be able to attract more people to buy on the basis of $10 than on the basis of $50.
That sounds as though it might be a commendable idea but one question which arises in all our minds is whether there is any move contemplated or any need for the expansion of the operations of the company. I think the best way to judge that would be to make a study of the company's operations. The company started operating in 1953 and I have before me both the annual report of the company for 1957, which gives a breakdown of operations from 1953 to 1957, and also the quarterly report for the first three months of this year. What do we find in the company's own report? If we study their actual daily deliveries we find that in 1953 the figure was 21,096 barrels, in 1954 it was 39,787 barrels, in 1955 it was 83,982 barrels, in 1956 it was 129,103 barrels and in 1957 it was 154,891 barrels. The annual highest average, therefore, works out to 154,891 barrels but as the officials pointed out to us, partly because of the recession, but particularly because of the United States policy with respect to oil, there has been a decline in their operations with the result that for the first three months of this year the average daily delivery of this pipe line is 102,180 barrels. And it looks as if on this delivery they are not losing money but still making it.
The reason I read this report, Mr. Speaker, was to show their low figure in 1954, their high in 1957, their present delivery rate, which is 102,000 barrels daily, and to ask you to relate that to the dumping capacity of the company, which according to the report is 250,000 barrels a day. Now, they have never come anywhere close to this capacity and on

the basis of their present operation they could carry on with their present equipment doing almost two and a quarter times the business they are doing today, and even on the basis of their high year of 1957 they would still have an additional capacity of approximately 100,000 barrels on a daily basis.
That being the situation according to the company's own figures, it seems highly improbable that in the foreseeable future they will have to go on the stock market in order to raise funds for the expansion of their delivery facilities, and the company has admitted that there is no such intention. So, on the basis outlined a few minutes ago of not issuing shares, on the basis of their facilities for increased business, we cannot see why there should be this pressure to have the House of Commons this session give the company the right to split their shares five to one.
I think that we, as public representatives, have the right to look very carefully into this situation and to ask the plain question whether or not this company, with its earnings and earning capacity, should be given this right to split its shares. Admittedly, in 1953 there was a loss in the first year of operations of $470,000, and in 1954 there was a loss of $1,256,000. But then they got into real operation and between 1955 and 1957, after all expenses, after all income tax, nearly $16 million was secured in net returns which added up in 1957 for example to net earnings per share of $5.52. Now $5.52 net earnings on what was basically a $10 share is quite a considerable return, and even on the basis of dividends paid out, which amounted to $2 a share, it was pretty good on $10. Of course, many of the shares were not purchased at $10 because of profit taking on the stock market, but even if they have not been sold on the stock market they are of that value to those who paid $10, which brings to my mind what happened with regard to Imperial Oil and other oil companies in this country.
The greatest and probably the only existing study ever made of share-splitting was made by the late Chief Justice M. A. Macdonald of British Columbia, who was appointed in 1934 as a royal commissioner to investigate the coal and petroleum industry. He filed his report in 1936, a most exhaustive report. I have a copy here and I regret that we have not time to read it into the record, because it is most interesting. One of the highlights of Mr. Justice Macdonald's findings concerned this matter of the oil companies and, in their operations, the splitting of shares in order to hide profits and in order to build up capital gains without the investment of new moneys. I will quote just one brief example of the Imperial Oil situation, and I take this directly from the report. It shows on page HH 251 a

table of the increases in authorized capital of Imperial Oil, which company, by the way, is a heavy shareholder in the Trans Mountain Oil Pipe Line Company; I believe it is one of the largest of the shareholders.
Equal with the other five major ones.

From 1880 to 1929 the capital of that company increased from $500,000, 5,000 shares of $100 each, to 32 million shares of no par value which, on the stock market, at a valuation in July of 1935, represented a value of $139,119,200. This was done, starting in 1913, by splitting shares; 150,000 into 500,000; 500,000 into 2 million; 2 million into 8 million; and 8 million into 32 million, with the result that the original share of $100 became worth $1,216 in July, 1935.
Mr. Justice Macdonald warned against the practice of splitting shares, and so, in view of what I have tried to point out from the company's own records, and in view of the history of the oil companies and of the profit derived by the method of splitting shares, we feel that the full story has not been told and that the reasons we have been given for the purport of this act cannot stand investigation.
I object to those words, Mr. Speaker.

We have come to the conclusion that our position is unchanged from the position we took in 1937 and we must again in this quarter of the house and in these circumstances oppose the House of Commons giving authority to this company to split the shares in the ratio of five to one.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I sat in
on the meeting the other day when the officials of the Trans Mountain Pipe Line Company consented to meet with a number of us to hear if there was any change in the attitude of the company compared with what it previously has been. I, personally, was very much interested in the fact that after they had talked for some time they informed us that this split from one share to five was not going to accomplish anything in the way of more money in the treasury. And I was particularly surprised to note that they maintained that they did not need any more money in the treasury, and that this was the only reason for this split. They have in the Trans Mountain Pipe Line Company 5,000,000 shares of no par value. Of these shares, about 1,000,000 have been issued, about 450,000 to private individuals.
If this company is interested in expansion and in raising more money for capital expenditures, then because of the value of the stock it would be a simple matter for it to raise the money by issuing some of
Private Bills
the treasury stocks it now holds to the general public. If the company wishes to raise more money it would appear logical for it to do so in the normal business practice. It could issue the stock it now has to the general public which would make available to the company enough money with which to expand and possibly make whatever investment it feels is necessary.
In the committee we asked why the company did not sell more stock. Frankly,
I was not impressed with its reasoning. Some hon. members may recall the history of this company. It came to parliament and asked to split its stock on one previous occasion. In the last application the main reason stated was that it wanted to split its stock again, not to eliminate the oil companies that are affected in the capitalization program, but because the company was distressed by the fact that the shares were rising on the market very rapidly and the profit of the company was becoming embarrassing in view of the small number of shares it had out. If this should be true it would appear that parliament is required to pass legislation to control the method of stock evaluation under which the profits can prove to be a source of embarrassment to the people who own the stock. In all fairness I must point out that when we asked the officials of the company about this matter they agreed they would also like to see legislation which would eliminate the necessity of their having to have these matters handled in this way.
I am in complete agreement that something must be done to control these companies. While their representatives pointed out that they are not similar to companies engaged in distributing gas, the situation over the years has developed to the point where federal legislation is required with respect to pipe line companies. The lack of legislation to control pipe lines is becoming more obvious to this parliament and the people of Canada every day. This applies not only to the federal field but to the provincial as well. The investigation into pipe line companies in Ontario has revealed that disastrous decimations have been made in the cabinet ranks of the legislature of that province.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Does the hon. member not think he is going a bit far afield? After all, we are dealing with the splitting of the stock of the Trans Mountain Pipe Line Company which does not operate in Ontario. May I suggest that the hon. member relate his remarks more closely to the subject of stock splitting.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I was attempting to suggest that the problem with

Private Bills
respect to this company is being reflected in other companies. The presumption would be that it will not be too long until some of the other pipe line companies for the same reason would have to come to this parliament to seek permission to split stock. If that is the solution to the problem which appears to have developed, then I can see other companies having to do the same thing.
I feel I am safe in saying that the company did not convince us that it had a legitimate reason for splitting its stock. Without regard to the fact that money was necessary the officials of the company pointed out they would like to have $40 million in their treasury for capital investment. They also pointed out that the capital investment was not going to take place immediately, that the splitting of the stock in itself was not a method of raising money for capital expenditures. The company did not have a program which, in my opinion, would indicate that it was going to increase its subsidiary industries that resulted from the establishment of the line in the Vancouver area. I do not think, therefore, there is much justification at the present time for this novel method of disposing of the high profits the company has been enjoying.
I feel it is basic common sense to say that if a company is making so much money that it is ashamed to face the Canadian people then the parliament of Canada should not play a part in concealing the matter in this way. If the company had come to parliament with a proposal for expanding industrial development in the immediate area of Vancouver or in the lower mainland of British Columbia then there might have been some justification for its application. The company stated independently that this would not allow them any additional money for that type of development so it could not be accomplished in this manner. I feel that this company should take another look at its method of disposing of stock. I feel the Canadian people are not much interested in seeing companies do this sort of thing. If the company issued the stock it has in its treasury for use in capital expenditures it would assist the Canadian economy but it is seeking only to split its stock in this fashion.
I wish to express my appreciation of the opportunity afforded me of meeting the officials of this company. With only a small investment this has become a large, economical company. These gentlemen came to Ottawa and by using a great deal of tact and finesse they pointed out, to me at least, the new trend that must be taking place in big business in terms of stock promotion and business operations. It is indeed a contrast with what occurs in the mining industry; in

fact, it could be described as being completely the reverse of what occurs there. In the mining industry instead of ending up with five shares for every one you find that you end up with one share for every five that you held and you are lucky if this does not happen several times a year. This appears to be stock splitting that is completely the reverse of the kind of stock splitting to which I am normally accustomed.
The mining industry, which has been splitting stocks for many years, in reverse, should take a look at the situation and in particular at the tactics these gentlemen use. It has been normal in the mining industry to tell my friends and me, yes, and other parliamentarians, this is the way it is going to be done, you can take it or you can leave it, and sometimes they have even offered some stock in the deal, but this appears-
How do you know?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I do not know it from firsthand knowledge because I have never had enough money to buy stock. Normally, stocksplitting involves something like this. Every time you buy one share of stock you end up with five or six for one. If this did not happen every time they came to parliament with a matter of this kind probably we would be more interested in buying stock.
Have you ever bought any stock?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I never have enough money to buy any stock.

Mr. Speaker, I hesitated in rising because I thought the hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Smith) was going to participate in this debate. I did, as did I am sure the hon. member who introduced this bill, look up past issues of Hansard in an attempt to familiarize myself with the background of a similar bill which was introduced in 1957. I noticed that at that time the then member for Victoria, Mr. Fairey, introduced the bill. In his introductory remarks, or in his remarks on second reading, he was very short. In fact, he said at that time that it was a simple bill and did not require too much expansion and he hoped that the bill would pass. Perhaps that was one of the reasons why he got into difficulty with the passage of it.
I would like to extend my congratulatory remarks to the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Broome), and not the least for expanding his remarks much farther than did his predecessor in introducing the bill. Even though he was more expansive and made more references to the structure of the company and its relationship with its employees, nevertheless I do not think he covered

adequately all of the ground or came anywhere near answering the objections which were raised when this bill was before parliament in 1957. In my opinion the questions which were raised at that time are still valid questions and still require answers.
I wonder, too, why this particular company, if this is the approach that they use-

May I ask a
question? Is this part of the speech of the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier) of last year or of Mr. Cameron's.
I did not catch the question.
Is this part of Mr. Cameron's or of the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam's speech of last June?
Mr. Cameron's.

I must admit we do have excellent taste. If this is the approach that Trans Mountain uses, I wonder why the company did not approach one of the members representing the Burnaby constituencies. I can well appreciate why they did not approach the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier) and ask him to introduce and support the bill, but I wonder why they had to go so far afield as Vancouver South to find someone to support and introduce this particular bill.
This is obviously part of the speech of the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, which he made last year.
It may be as my hon. friend says.
Why does the hon. member not ask me if I make my own speeches?

In any event, Mr. Speaker, with respect to the comments made by hon. members opposite, when I opened my remarks I said the hon. member for Vancouver South did not come anywhere near answering the questions which were raised during the debate on this bill a year ago, and did not come anywhere near dealing with the objections which were raised at that time. Inasmuch as the subject matter of the bill is the same, and inasmuch as it was given a most exhaustive debate and study a year ago, where else would one go than to the past records of Hansard to see what the problem is all about. Actually, in reading those references in Hansard, just as we do in other research work in attempting to deal with other problems, we must deal with points that were dealt with in the speeches and debates of the past.

The Tories should do their
homework, too.

If the remarks that I am making now and the remarks that I intend to make about this bill in the future are similar to remarks made by hon. members of this house in previous debates, or by present hon. members, well, it is only natural that they should be so.
In the operation of pipe lines, whether they be gas or oil, the hon. member for Vancouver South attempted to differentiate between the two and to say that the promoters, owners and operators of oil pipe lines were lily white pure compared with the buccaneers and pirates interested in the operation of gas pipe lines. Be that as it may, we have seen over the years that both oil pipe lines and gas pipe lines, in the operation of the oil and gas industry, have done nothing but enrich the pockets of a number of promoters. It has been a most lucrative industry-the gas pipe lines and the oil pipe lines-both here in Canada and in the United States.

Will the hon. member permit a question? Is he not aware that not one cent was made in promotion fees in the promotion of the Trans Mountain Oil Pipe Line Company? In reading the prospectus I tried to point out that every cent raised went into the treasury of the company and was used for the development of the company.
What was the question?
Six o'clock.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: On Monday, Mr. Speaker, we intend to take a supply motion. If we get into supply we shall go on with trade and commerce.

May I ask the Minister of
Public Works whether he does not feel that, according to the rule book of this house, it would be more appropriate to take a private member's motion, which would be just a second day for private members' bills, rather than one supply motion following another?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker; I think it is more important under existing conditions to have a supply motion.
